===== FILE: configs/architecture.yaml =====
title: Personalized Pricing System
tagline: Channels → gateway → identity → features → PDS → log → learn → gate → serve.
about: >
  This is the full loop. Channels ask for a price. The edge authenticates and
  screens bots. Identity and the feature store build context. The Pricing
  Decision Service applies guardrails, scores arms, and picks one. Every
  decision is logged with a propensity. Outcomes join later. Offline learning
  trains, evaluates (OPE), and only then may a model climb back into live
  traffic. The pieces below include what a complete system needs that a
  “brain-only” diagram often leaves out: catalog/cost, inventory, coupons,
  experiment holdout, feature registry, CS explainability, monitoring,
  control-plane kill switch, sticky prices, offer ledger, and batch campaigns.
in_short: >
  Online path returns a price in <100ms. Offline path turns (x, a, p, r)
  into a gated model. The control plane can freeze, honor, or roll it back.
added_vs_typical_brain_diagram:
  - Product catalog / cost / MAP / MSRP service
  - Inventory & supply signals
  - Coupon / offer / entitlement service
  - Experiment platform (holdout A/B vs bandit vs shadow)
  - Feature registry (name, type, freshness, owner)
  - Policy-as-code / config service (guardrails, ladders, versions)
  - Consent & preference center
  - Explainability / CS lookup by decision_id
  - Outcome event API (view, cart, purchase, refund)
  - Monitoring, PSI drift, fairness parity, auto-rollback
  - Finance reconciliation (quoted vs collected vs refunded)
  - Circuit breakers and static-price fallback
  - Human override (merchandiser / sales approval for B2B)
gaps_in_original_doc:
  - title: Control plane (kill switch / freeze / promo calendar)
    why: A merchandiser or SRE must stop personalization in seconds without a redeploy. The original diagram has fallbacks but no human override bus.
  - title: Session & cross-channel price stickiness
    why: The same shopper must not see $39.99 on mobile and $44.99 on desktop ten minutes later. Cart integrity and perceived fairness depend on a TTL lock.
  - title: Offer ledger (honor issued prices)
    why: An emailed coupon is a contract. Policy updates must not void a code that was already shown. Ledger ≠ creative binding.
  - title: Global discount & exploration budget
    why: Per-customer frequency caps do not protect the P&L. Daily promotional spend and exploration share need a knapsack.
  - title: Batch / campaign scoring path
    why: Email and ads are not request/response. They need a batch decide() with the same contracts, logged propensities, and offer TTL.
  - title: Tax / FX / localization
    why: Post-process mentioned currency in one line. Tax-inclusive markets and CAD/EUR display are a separate service.
  - title: Online vs offline feature skew
    why: Training x and serving x diverge silently. PSI on features (not just propensity) is a first-class SLO.
  - title: Action-space versioning
    why: If discount ladders change, old propensities are invalid for OPE. candidate_set_version must be a contract, not a log decoration.
  - title: Multi-objective reward
    why: E[Revenue|x,p] is one of several Y's — margin, LTV, inventory burn, refund risk. The reward contract must name the mix.
  - title: PII minimization, retention, legal hold
    why: Experience tuples contain context. Training must strip PII; protected attributes are logged for audit and never enter x.
  - title: Search / listing price consistency
    why: The grid price must match the PDP price for the same session or shoppers bounce. Not only a PDP use case.
  - title: Cross-SKU cannibalization
    why: Discounting earbuds can steal headphone margin. A per-SKU bandit is myopic without a basket or category model.
  - title: Fraud / payment-risk coupling
    why: Deep discounts on high-refund or stolen-card cohorts burn cash. Risk score should tighten guardrails, not train the bandit.
  - title: Attribution & delayed conversion window
    why: Join-later is named but not owned. Who closes the reward window, handles multi-touch, and censors open sessions?
layers:
  - id: channels
    title: Client / channels
    purpose: Where a price is shown and where outcomes start.
    pieces: [Web PDP, Mobile, Email / push, Ads, POS / call center, Partner / B2B API]
  - id: gateway
    title: Edge / API gateway
    purpose: Cross-cutting checks before any pricing logic.
    pieces: [Auth & session, Rate limit, Geo & device, Bot score, Experiment routing]
  - id: identity
    title: Identity & context
    purpose: Who is this shopper, and may we personalize?
    pieces: [Identity graph, Session stitch, Segment service, Consent / GDPR]
  - id: features
    title: Feature store
    purpose: Low-latency x for inference; point-in-time x for training.
    pieces: [Online Redis, Offline lake, Stream jobs, Feature registry]
  - id: catalog
    title: Catalog, cost, inventory
    purpose: Legal and economic facts the model may not invent.
    pieces: [List / MAP / MSRP, Cost, Stock, Competitor feed]
  - id: pds
    title: Pricing Decision Service
    purpose: Guardrails → candidates → causal μ,σ → bandit → offer.
    pieces: [Eligibility, Causal, Bandit, Post-process, Fallback, Cache]
  - id: offers
    title: Coupon & creative
    purpose: Bind a price to a redeemable, expiring offer and copy.
    pieces: [Coupon issue, Badge / CTA, TTL, Entitlements]
  - id: logging
    title: Logging & event bus
    purpose: Persist (x, a, p) then join r. 100% of decisions, async.
    pieces: [Kafka decisions, Kafka outcomes, Schema registry, Lakehouse]
  - id: offline
    title: Offline learning
    purpose: Train, OPE, register, gate — never on the hot path.
    pieces: [Ingest, Join, Backfill, Causal, Bandit, OPE, Registry, Gate]
  - id: experiments
    title: Experiment platform
    purpose: Holdout A/B for clean causal estimates; bandit on the rest.
    pieces: [Assignment, Holdout, Shadow, Canary / ramp]
  - id: monitor
    title: Monitoring & feedback
    purpose: Latency, reward vs μ, propensity drift, fairness, rollback.
    pieces: [SLIs, PSI, Parity, Live KPI vs control]
  - id: control
    title: Control plane
    purpose: Stop, freeze, or budget personalization without a redeploy.
    pieces: [Kill switch, Merchandiser freeze, Promo calendar, Discount budget]
  - id: consistency
    title: Price consistency & offer ledger
    purpose: Same shopper, same SKU, same price — and honor what was already shown.
    pieces: [Sticky TTL, Offer ledger, Redemption, Search/PDP match]
  - id: batch
    title: Batch / campaign scoring
    purpose: Score email, ads, and CRM lists with the same contracts as the hot path.
    pieces: [decide_batch, Offer TTL, Propensity log, Frequency cap]
  - id: privacy
    title: Privacy, audit, localization
    purpose: PII stays out of x; tax/FX are applied after the policy; logs expire.
    pieces: [Consent, Retention, Protected-attr audit, Tax / FX]
  - id: support
    title: Explainability / CS
    purpose: Look up a decision_id without exposing model guts to shoppers.
    pieces: [Reason codes, Decision lookup, Audit export]
loops:
  online:
    - Channel sends context (SKU, session, device, geo)
    - Gateway auth, rate-limits, scores bots, assigns experiment
    - Control plane may kill-switch, freeze, or exhaust budget → list price
    - Identity resolves guest vs account and consent
    - Feature store returns online x; catalog/inventory attach constraints
    - Sticky TTL may replay the last offer for this shopper × SKU
    - Guardrails filter arms; causal scores; bandit picks; coupon + ledger bind
    - Tax / FX localize the display price; async log (x, a, p, versions)
  offline:
    - Ingest decisions + outcomes; quarantine bad schema
    - Join & label reward; censor open windows; clip propensity
    - Point-in-time backfill; leakage check
    - Causal + bandit train; fairness + PSI
    - OPE vs current; registry; deployment gate
  feedback:
    - Outcomes POST joins r onto decision_id
    - Gate pass → shadow → canary → ramp
    - KPI drop / PSI / fairness / latency → auto-rollback
    - In-flight requests keep pinned versions
contracts:
  feature:
    name: string
    type: numeric or categorical
    freshness_ttl: seconds
    owner: team
  decision:
    context_schema: x_raw
    action_space: arms
    action_space_version: candidate_set_version
    propensity: "(0, 1]"
  reward:
    event: purchase
    window_days: 7
    net_of: refunds
    definition: margin
    multi_objective: "0.5 rev + 0.3 margin + 0.2 ltv"
  offer:
    honor: issued codes survive policy change
    sticky_ttl_seconds: 1800
    redeem_once: true
nfrs:
  latency_p99_ms: 100
  throughput_rps: 10000
  availability: 0.9995
  logging_completeness: 1.0
  model_freshness_online: seconds
  model_freshness_offline: daily
try: Open Architecture, then run a use case. Close the loop with an outcome event and the monitor.


===== FILE: configs/azure_architecture.yaml =====
title: Azure architecture for this pricing lab
tagline: Same pricing service. Azure hosts, stores, logs, trains, and gates it.
about: >
  This project decides a price for a shopper and SKU in under 100 ms, logs the
  decision with a propensity, then trains offline. Azure does not replace that
  logic. It replaces the local stand-ins: process hosting, cache, database,
  event bus, lakehouse, model registry, and control-plane flags. Region is
  Canada Central so personal data stays in Canada.
in_short: >
  Channel → Front Door → APIM → Container Apps (PDS) → Redis + Cosmos →
  Event Hubs → ADLS → Azure ML (OPE gate) → canary revision.
try: Open Azure → Overview, then Architecture diagram, then CLI commands.
layers:
  - title: Front Door
    purpose: TLS, geo routing, and WAF/bot filtering in front of the API.
    tool: Azure Front Door + WAF
    maps_to: Gateway / bot / geo
  - title: API Management
    purpose: Auth, rate limits, and product split so /v1/price is public and /explain is not.
    tool: Azure API Management
    maps_to: Rate limit, public vs explain routes
  - title: Container Apps
    purpose: Runs the FastAPI Pricing Decision Service (stages 0–10) with replica scale and revision traffic split.
    tool: Azure Container Apps
    maps_to: Pricing Decision Service stages 0–10
  - title: App Configuration
    purpose: Kill switch, freeze, version pins, and budget without a new image.
    tool: Azure App Configuration
    maps_to: Kill switch / freeze / versions
  - title: Key Vault
    purpose: Stores connection strings and keys. The app reads them via managed identity.
    tool: Azure Key Vault
    maps_to: Secrets
  - title: Redis
    purpose: Sub-millisecond online features, sticky price TTL, frequency caps, and spend counters.
    tool: Azure Cache for Redis
    maps_to: Feature store + sticky price
  - title: Cosmos DB
    purpose: Catalog (list/MAP/cost/stock), identity, offer ledger, and decision lookup.
    tool: Azure Cosmos DB
    maps_to: Catalog, identity, offer ledger
  - title: Event Hubs
    purpose: Async log of every (context, action, propensity) and later outcomes. Kafka protocol.
    tool: Azure Event Hubs (Kafka mode)
    maps_to: Decision + outcome logs
  - title: Storage (ADLS)
    purpose: Lakehouse for bronze capture, silver joined training rows, gold OPE reports.
    tool: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2
    maps_to: Lakehouse bronze/silver/gold
  - title: Azure ML
    purpose: Offline causal/bandit training, OPE evaluation, model registry, promotion gate.
    tool: Azure Machine Learning
    maps_to: Causal, bandit, OPE, registry, gate
  - title: Monitor
    purpose: Latency, error rate, completeness, fairness, and automatic revision rollback.
    tool: App Insights + Azure Monitor
    maps_to: Latency, fairness, rollback

# Bill of materials for Personalized Pricing on Azure.
# required: must | should | later
# week: 1–8 matching the implementation plan

groups:
  - id: foundation
    title: Foundation
    about: Subscription, grouping, logs, identity. Create these before any app.
  - id: hosting
    title: Hosting
    about: Where the Pricing Decision Service actually runs.
  - id: config
    title: Config and secrets
    about: Kill switch and credentials. No secrets in source or container env files in prod.
  - id: online_data
    title: Online data plane
    about: Lookups on the hot path (p99 under 100 ms).
  - id: streaming
    title: Streaming and lakehouse
    about: Every decision logged with propensity; outcomes join later.
  - id: ml
    title: Machine learning
    about: Train, evaluate (OPE), register, promote. Never train on Container Apps.
  - id: edge
    title: Public edge
    about: Add when a real channel calls you. Skip for the first internal deploy.
  - id: observe
    title: Observability and rollback
    about: You cannot run a bandit without completeness, latency, and fairness signals.
  - id: security
    title: Security and Canada compliance
    about: PIPEDA, private networking, classification.
  - id: cicd
    title: CI/CD
    about: Test, image, revision. Failed pytest never deploys.
  - id: optional
    title: Optional later
    about: Only if scale, Spark volume, or email campaigns require them.

components:
  - id: subscription
    group: foundation
    required: must
    week: 1
    name: Azure subscription
    tool: Microsoft Entra + Azure billing
    replaces: nothing — this is the account
    purpose: Billing boundary and permission root. Use a dedicated dev subscription first.
    sku_dev: Pay-as-you-go or Visual Studio credit
    sku_prod: Enterprise Agreement or MCA, separate prod subscription
    how: az login then az account show. Confirm you have Contributor.
    pitfall: Do not mix prod pricing data into a personal subscription.

  - id: entra
    group: foundation
    required: must
    week: 1
    name: Microsoft Entra ID
    tool: Entra ID (directory)
    replaces: nothing
    purpose: Human login (az login, portal) and workload identity for the Container App.
    sku_dev: Included
    sku_prod: PIM for privileged roles
    how: Default tenant of the subscription. Later assign roles to the app's managed identity.
    pitfall: Do not put long-lived client secrets in GitHub. Use OIDC federation.

  - id: rg
    group: foundation
    required: must
    week: 1
    name: Resource group
    tool: Azure Resource Manager
    replaces: the whole local project folder as a cloud lifecycle unit
    purpose: One named box in Canada Central. Create, tag, and delete together.
    sku_dev: n/a
    sku_prod: n/a
    how: az group create -n rg-pds-canadacentral-dev -l canadacentral
    pitfall: Creating resources in East US by habit. Always pass --location canadacentral.

  - id: budget
    group: foundation
    required: must
    week: 1
    name: Cost Management budget
    tool: Azure Cost Management
    replaces: nothing
    purpose: Email when spend crosses a cap so a forgotten Event Hub does not surprise you.
    sku_dev: $400/month alert
    sku_prod: agreed prod cap
    how: az consumption budget create --amount 400 --resource-group $RG ...
    pitfall: Budgets alert; they do not always stop resources by themselves.

  - id: logs
    group: foundation
    required: must
    week: 1
    name: Log Analytics workspace
    tool: Azure Monitor
    replaces: local terminal output
    purpose: Container Apps, APIM, and App Insights all dump here. One workspace per env.
    sku_dev: Pay-as-you-go, 30-day retention
    sku_prod: 90–400 day retention to match reward/legal window
    how: az monitor log-analytics workspace create
    pitfall: Multiple workspaces make queries impossible. Share one per environment.

  - id: appi
    group: observe
    required: must
    week: 2
    name: Application Insights
    tool: Azure Monitor Application Insights
    replaces: metrics.py in-process counters for production APM
    purpose: Request duration (p99), dependency calls to Redis/Cosmos, exceptions, live metrics.
    sku_dev: Workspace-based, default
    sku_prod: Sampling if volume is high; keep 100% of /v1/price failures
    how: az monitor app-insights component create --workspace $LA
    pitfall: Logging propensity or PII in custom events. Log decision_id only on the public path.

  - id: acr
    group: hosting
    required: must
    week: 1
    name: Azure Container Registry
    tool: ACR
    replaces: "docker images sitting only on your laptop"
    purpose: Stores pds-api:v0.1.0 (and git SHA tags). Container Apps pulls from here.
    sku_dev: Basic
    sku_prod: Standard or Premium (geo-replication Canada East later)
    how: az acr create --sku Basic; docker push
    pitfall: ACR name is globally unique. Admin user is fine in dev; prod uses managed identity pull.

  - id: cae
    group: hosting
    required: must
    week: 1
    name: Container Apps environment
    tool: Azure Container Apps
    replaces: "uvicorn on 127.0.0.1"
    purpose: The cluster your app replicas join. Attach Log Analytics at create time.
    sku_dev: Consumption
    sku_prod: Workload profiles, zone redundant
    how: az containerapp env create
    pitfall: Creating the app without an environment. Always create env first.

  - id: ca
    group: hosting
    required: must
    week: 1
    name: Container App (PDS)
    tool: Azure Container Apps
    replaces: python -m uvicorn ... --port 8080
    purpose: Runs stages 0–10. Scale 1–N replicas. Revisions + traffic split = shadow/canary.
    sku_dev: 0.5 vCPU / 1 Gi, min 1 max 3
    sku_prod: 1 vCPU / 2 Gi, min 3, max 30, HTTP concurrency tuned to p99
    how: az containerapp create --target-port 8080 --ingress external (dev) or internal (prod)
    pitfall: Exposing /v1/price:explain, /v1/control, /v1/admin/reload on public ingress.

  - id: ca_job
    group: hosting
    required: should
    week: 6
    name: Container Apps Job
    tool: Azure Container Apps Jobs
    replaces: POST /v1/price:batch from a laptop loop
    purpose: Overnight campaign scoring (email/CRM lists) with the same decide() contracts.
    sku_dev: Manual trigger
    sku_prod: Scheduled cron, 1–2 vCPU
    how: az containerapp job create --trigger-type Schedule
    pitfall: Hammering /v1/price one-by-one from Logic Apps without backpressure.

  - id: identity_mi
    group: config
    required: must
    week: 2
    name: Managed identity
    tool: System-assigned identity on the Container App
    replaces: connection strings in .env files
    purpose: The app gets a badge. Key Vault and App Config grant that badge a role. No secret in the image.
    sku_dev: System-assigned
    sku_prod: User-assigned if multiple apps share Key Vault
    how: az containerapp identity assign --system-assigned then role assignment
    pitfall: Still embedding Cosmos keys in --env-vars after identity is on.

  - id: kv
    group: config
    required: must
    week: 2
    name: Key Vault
    tool: Azure Key Vault
    replaces: hardcoded secrets
    purpose: Redis URL, Cosmos key (until AAD), Event Hubs send string, App Insights connection string.
    sku_dev: Standard
    sku_prod: Standard, RBAC, purge protection, private endpoint
    how: az keyvault create --enable-rbac-authorization true
    pitfall: Access policies mixed with RBAC. Pick RBAC and stick to it.

  - id: appcs
    group: config
    required: must
    week: 2
    name: App Configuration
    tool: Azure App Configuration
    replaces: configs/control_plane.yaml and configs/versions.yaml for runtime flags
    purpose: pds.kill_switch, merchandiser_freeze, policy_id, causal_model_id, daily_discount_budget. Refresh in seconds.
    sku_dev: Free
    sku_prod: Standard, replica in Canada East
    how: az appconfig create; az appconfig feature set --feature pds.kill_switch
    pitfall: If App Config is unreachable, fail closed to list price using last cached flags (max 60s).

  - id: redis
    group: online_data
    required: must
    week: 3
    name: Azure Cache for Redis
    tool: Azure Cache for Redis
    replaces: services/feature_store.py dict and StickyPriceStore
    purpose: feat:{id}, sticky:{id}:{sku} TTL 1800s, freq caps, budget INCR. Target GET under 2 ms.
    sku_dev: Basic C0 (TLS 6380)
    sku_prod: Premium P1, zone redundant, Redis 6+, private endpoint
    how: az redis create --sku Basic --vm-size C0
    pitfall: Non-SSL port. Always rediss:// on 6380. If Redis is down, degrade features, still return a price.

  - id: cosmos
    group: online_data
    required: must
    week: 4
    name: Azure Cosmos DB
    tool: Cosmos DB NoSQL
    replaces: configs/catalog.yaml, identity profiles, coupon.ledger, decision lookup
    purpose: Containers catalog (/sku), customers (/customer_id), offers (/code), decisions (/customer_id).
    sku_dev: Serverless
    sku_prod: Autoscale 1000–4000 RU, periodic backup, Canada East failover
    how: az cosmosdb create --capabilities EnableServerless then four sql containers
    pitfall: One huge container with no partition key. Offers must survive policy change (ledger, not cache).

  - id: evh_ns
    group: streaming
    required: must
    week: 5
    name: Event Hubs namespace
    tool: Event Hubs with Kafka enabled
    replaces: data/log_buffer/decisions.jsonl
    purpose: Kafka-compatible bus so the existing “topic + propensity” design stays. Capture to ADLS.
    sku_dev: Standard, 1 TU
    sku_prod: Premium, 4+ PU, zone redundant
    how: az eventhubs namespace create --sku Standard --enable-kafka true
    pitfall: Using Service Bus queues instead. This workload is high-volume telemetry, not a command queue.

  - id: evh_decisions
    group: streaming
    required: must
    week: 5
    name: Hub pricing.decisions.v1
    tool: Event Hub
    replaces: DecisionLogger JSONL
    purpose: One event per decide(). Fields include propensity, policy_id, candidate_set_version, variant.
    sku_dev: 8 partitions, 7-day retention
    sku_prod: partition count sized to 10k+ rps, capture on
    how: az eventhubs eventhub create -n pricing.decisions.v1 --partition-count 8
    pitfall: Logging without propensity. OPE becomes fiction. If the hub is down, buffer and force exploit.

  - id: evh_outcomes
    group: streaming
    required: must
    week: 5
    name: Hub pricing.outcomes.v1
    tool: Event Hub
    replaces: POST /v1/outcomes local lake
    purpose: purchase, refund, return keyed by decision_id. Joined later with a 7-day window, net of refunds.
    sku_dev: 4 partitions
    sku_prod: match checkout volume
    how: az eventhubs eventhub create -n pricing.outcomes.v1
    pitfall: Joining on customer_id only. Always join on decision_id.

  - id: schema
    group: streaming
    required: should
    week: 5
    name: Schema Registry
    tool: Azure Schema Registry (Event Hubs)
    replaces: implicit JSON shape in Python
    purpose: Version the experience tuple. Breaking changes get a new schema version, not silent field drops.
    sku_dev: Included with Standard namespace
    sku_prod: same, with compatibility checks in CI
    how: Create registry in the Event Hubs namespace in portal or ARM
    pitfall: Changing ladders without bumping candidate_set_version. Old propensities become invalid for OPE.

  - id: adls
    group: streaming
    required: must
    week: 5
    name: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2
    tool: Storage account with hierarchical namespace
    replaces: data/lake/*.jsonl
    purpose: bronze/decisions, bronze/outcomes, silver/training, silver/backfill, gold/ope, gold/campaigns.
    sku_dev: Standard LRS, HNS on
    sku_prod: ZRS or GRS, lifecycle to match retention, private endpoint
    how: az storage account create --enable-hierarchical-namespace true
    pitfall: A plain blob account without HNS. Spark/Delta expects a lake, not a dump folder.

  - id: capture
    group: streaming
    required: must
    week: 5
    name: Event Hubs Capture
    tool: Capture to ADLS
    replaces: a custom consumer you would otherwise write on day one
    purpose: Lands bronze JSON/Avro on a schedule so ML jobs have files even if no Spark job is running yet.
    sku_dev: 5-minute interval
    sku_prod: 5-minute, size-based flush
    how: az eventhubs eventhub update --enable-capture true --storage-account-resource-id ...
    pitfall: Capture destination in another region.

  - id: mlw
    group: ml
    required: must
    week: 6
    name: Azure Machine Learning workspace
    tool: Azure ML
    replaces: data/registry/models.json and ad-hoc numpy jobs on the laptop
    purpose: Job submit for causal/bandit/OPE, model registry, environment images, lineage.
    sku_dev: Default workspace + serverless jobs
    sku_prod: Dedicated compute cluster off-peak, private network
    how: az ml workspace create --storage-account $STG
    pitfall: Training inside the online Container App. That path must stay hot and stateless.

  - id: ml_compute
    group: ml
    required: should
    week: 6
    name: Azure ML compute (serverless or cluster)
    tool: Azure ML compute
    replaces: running OfflinePipeline on your PC
    purpose: CPU is enough for the current numpy/ridge learners. GPU only if you swap in a neural bandit later.
    sku_dev: Serverless
    sku_prod: Cluster, scale to zero
    how: az ml compute create or job serverless
    pitfall: Leaving a GPU cluster on overnight.

  - id: spark
    group: ml
    required: should
    week: 6
    name: Microsoft Fabric or Azure Databricks
    tool: Spark
    replaces: offline/join.py and backfill.py once volume exceeds single-node pandas/numpy
    purpose: Point-in-time feature join at scale, leakage checks, Delta tables.
    sku_dev: Skip; use Azure ML single node on the JSONL/Delta sample
    sku_prod: Fabric Spark or Databricks in Canada Central, reading ADLS
    how: Create workspace; mount adls://lake
    pitfall: Training on “current” features instead of as-of decision timestamp.

  - id: fd
    group: edge
    required: should
    week: 8
    name: Azure Front Door
    tool: Front Door Premium
    replaces: nothing locally (dev uses Container Apps FQDN)
    purpose: Anycast, TLS, WAF bot manager, origin health, Canada POP.
    sku_dev: Skip
    sku_prod: Premium + WAF
    how: Create profile, origin group = APIM or Container Apps
    pitfall: Pointing Front Door at the explain endpoint.

  - id: waf
    group: edge
    required: should
    week: 8
    name: WAF / bot manager
    tool: Front Door WAF policy
    replaces: services/gateway.py bot_score as the only defense
    purpose: Block scrapers so you do not waste exploration on bots.
    sku_dev: Skip
    sku_prod: Prevention mode after a week of Detection
    how: Attach policy to Front Door
    pitfall: Prevention on day one with no allowlist for partner IPs.

  - id: apim
    group: edge
    required: should
    week: 8
    name: API Management
    tool: Azure API Management
    replaces: gateway rate limit and route policy
    purpose: Products — public (POST /v1/price), checkout identity (outcomes), CS (decision lookup), internal (explain/control).
    sku_dev: Skip or Developer (not SLA)
    sku_prod: Standard v2 or Premium VNet
    how: az apim create --sku-name StandardV2
    pitfall: Developer SKU in production. It has no SLA and is expensive for what you get.

  - id: alerts
    group: observe
    required: must
    week: 2
    name: Metric alerts and action group
    tool: Azure Monitor alerts
    replaces: watching the terminal
    purpose: p99 > 100 ms, 5xx, Event Hub lag vs request count, kill-switch stale, fairness gap.
    sku_dev: Email action group
    sku_prod: Email + Teams + on-call
    how: az monitor action-group create; az monitor metrics alert create
    pitfall: Alerts with no owner. Name the person in the action group.

  - id: workbook
    group: observe
    required: should
    week: 7
    name: Azure Monitor workbook
    tool: Workbooks
    replaces: the lab Monitor tab for production
    purpose: Reward vs predicted μ, propensity PSI, segment price gap, logging completeness.
    sku_dev: Optional
    sku_prod: Pinned dashboard
    how: Create workbook on the Log Analytics workspace
    pitfall: Dashboards on sampled telemetry only.

  - id: vnet
    group: security
    required: should
    week: 8
    name: Virtual network + private endpoints
    tool: Azure VNet, Private Link
    replaces: public data-plane endpoints in dev
    purpose: Redis, Cosmos, Key Vault, Storage, Event Hubs not on the public internet in prod.
    sku_dev: Skip
    sku_prod: Required
    how: VNet, subnets, private endpoints, Container Apps VNet integration
    pitfall: Private endpoints without DNS. The app will hang on names.

  - id: purview
    group: security
    required: should
    week: 8
    name: Microsoft Purview
    tool: Purview
    replaces: nothing in the lab
    purpose: Scan ADLS, classify PII, restrict who can read bronze decisions.
    sku_dev: Skip
    sku_prod: Governance required for PIPEDA evidence
    how: Register ADLS source, scan, collections
    pitfall: Protected attributes leaking into feature columns. Policy-deny unexpected fields.

  - id: defender
    group: security
    required: should
    week: 8
    name: Defender for Cloud
    tool: Microsoft Defender for Cloud
    replaces: nothing
    purpose: Misconfig (public Cosmos, no TLS on Redis), container vulnerabilities on ACR images.
    sku_dev: Free posture
    sku_prod: Defender CSPM + containers
    how: Enable on the subscription
    pitfall: Ignoring registry scan failures and still deploying.

  - id: oidc
    group: cicd
    required: must
    week: 1
    name: GitHub Actions OIDC
    tool: Entra app federation
    replaces: deploying from a laptop
    purpose: pytest → docker build → ACR → Container Apps revision. No PAT in secrets.
    sku_dev: GitHub-hosted runner
    sku_prod: same, environment protection on prod
    how: Federated credential on an Entra app; azure/login@v2
    pitfall: AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET in GitHub. Use OIDC instead.

  - id: aks
    group: optional
    required: later
    week: 8
    name: Azure Kubernetes Service
    tool: AKS
    replaces: Container Apps only if you outgrow it (sustained >10k rps, custom mesh)
    purpose: Extra control. Not the first hosting choice.
    sku_dev: Do not start here
    sku_prod: Only with a platform team
    how: n/a until needed
    pitfall: Starting on AKS “because Kubernetes.” You will spend weeks on YAML instead of OPE.

  - id: appservice
    group: optional
    required: later
    week: 1
    name: App Service (not recommended as primary)
    tool: Azure App Service
    replaces: Container Apps
    purpose: Acceptable only as a throwaway demo. Weak revision/canary compared with Container Apps.
    sku_dev: Avoid
    sku_prod: Avoid
    how: Do not
    pitfall: Using App Service slots as a substitute for propensity-logged canary.

  - id: servicebus
    group: optional
    required: later
    week: 5
    name: Service Bus (not for decision logs)
    tool: Azure Service Bus
    replaces: nothing in this design
    purpose: Fine for commands (e.g. “rebuild features”). Wrong for 10k decisions/sec telemetry.
    sku_dev: n/a
    sku_prod: n/a
    how: Do not use instead of Event Hubs
    pitfall: Choosing Service Bus because it is familiar.

  - id: acs
    group: optional
    required: later
    week: 7
    name: Azure Communication Services
    tool: ACS Email
    replaces: whatever sends win-back mail
    purpose: Optional if you have no ESP. Campaign job writes offers; ACS or SendGrid sends.
    sku_dev: Skip
    sku_prod: Only if you lack an ESP
    how: After decide_batch has offer codes
    pitfall: Sending a price that is not in the offer ledger.

===== FILE: configs/offline_stages.yaml =====
- id: ol_overview
  number: null
  title: Offline overview
  tagline: Learn from logs. Never in the checkout hot path.
  about: >
    The online Pricing Decision Service answers in tens of milliseconds.
    This pipeline is the night shift. It reads yesterday’s decisions and
    purchases, builds better models, estimates whether a new policy would
    have made more money, and only then is allowed near live traffic.
  in_short: >
    Kafka-style logs in → join, train, evaluate, gate → a candidate model
    out. Checkout never waits on this work.
  process:
    - title: Collect what happened
      detail: >
        Decision logs (who saw which price, and the propensity) and outcome
        logs (who bought, refunded, or left) land in a lakehouse. Here that
        lake is local JSONL files. In production it is Iceberg/Delta on S3.
    - title: Turn logs into a training table
      detail: >
        We join outcomes onto decisions, compute a reward (default: margin),
        hide rows that are still waiting for a purchase, and refuse rows
        with a missing propensity — those cannot be used for honest
        off-policy evaluation.
    - title: Train, then prove it, then ship
      detail: >
        A causal model learns expected reward. A bandit update refreshes
        exploration posteriors. OPE estimates the new policy’s value without
        deploying it. The registry stores the artifact. The gate says yes
        or no. Yes means shadow → canary → ramp, never a big-bang cutover.
  try: Open Ingestion and seed history, then walk the tabs in order. This overview refreshes the lake counts.

- id: ol_ingest
  number: 1
  title: Ingestion
  tagline: Land decisions and outcomes in the lake, once each.
  about: >
    Two streams matter most: pricing.decisions.v1 (the experience tuple)
    and pricing.outcomes.v1 (view, cart, purchase, refund). Ingestion is
    boring on purpose. If we double-count a decision or drop a schema, every
    later number is a lie.
  in_short: >
    Read logs, drop PII, keep the first copy of each decision_id, quarantine
    broken rows, accept late outcomes.
  process:
    - title: Read the decision topic
      detail: >
        Each row is one checkout price: context features, candidate arms,
        chosen arm, propensity, version pins, degraded flag. We also pull
        any live JSONL the online service already wrote.
    - title: Deduplicate by decision_id
      detail: >
        Kafka is at-least-once. The same decision may arrive twice. We keep
        the first and count the rest as duplicates. Training on duplicates
        would pretend we had more data than we do.
    - title: Quarantine schema mismatches
      detail: >
        A row without decision_id, chosen_arm, or propensity cannot join or
        evaluate. It goes to a quarantine table and an alert, not into the
        training set.
    - title: Store outcomes separately
      detail: >
        Purchases may arrive hours later. They live in their own table keyed
        by the same decision_id so the next job can upsert a late refund
        without rewriting history incorrectly.
  try: Set “seed decisions” to 80 and run. You should see inserted decisions plus simulated purchases.

- id: ol_join
  number: 2
  title: Join & labeling
  tagline: Attach “did they buy?” and compute the reward.
  about: >
    A decision without an outcome is half a sentence. This job left-joins
    outcomes onto decisions and writes a single number the models optimize:
    the reward. Default reward is margin. You can switch to revenue or a
    composite to see how labels change.
  in_short: >
    Join on decision_id, apply an attribution window, net out refunds, clip
    bad propensities, mask rows that are still too new to judge.
  process:
    - title: Join decisions to outcomes
      detail: >
        One decision can have several events (view, cart, purchase, refund).
        We take the first purchase as the main outcome. A later refund
        subtracts from revenue and margin so we do not celebrate a sale that
        came back.
    - title: Respect the attribution window
      detail: >
        A purchase counted for 7 days, a refund for 30. If the decision is
        only two hours old and nobody bought yet, the row is censored — we
        do not treat “no purchase yet” as “will never buy”. Those rows are
        hidden from training until the window closes.
    - title: Compute the pinned reward
      detail: >
        Margin = price − cost on a purchase (or 0). Revenue = price.
        LTV-proxy down-weights high-churn shoppers. Composite blends the
        three. The same window of data must not mix reward definitions.
    - title: Validate propensity
      detail: >
        Propensity must sit in (0, 1]. Missing or zero → exclude from OPE.
        Tiny values are clipped to ε (0.01) so 1/propensity does not explode.
        Degraded online decisions are flagged so they do not teach the next
        model the fallback policy.
  try: Switch reward type from margin to revenue and compare the sample labels.

- id: ol_backfill
  number: 3
  title: Feature backfill
  tagline: Use features as they were at decision time — not today.
  about: >
    The online feature store shows who the customer is *now*. Training on
    today’s LTV to explain yesterday’s purchase is leakage: the model peeks
    at the future and looks brilliant offline, then fails live. We prefer
    the features already logged on the decision.
  in_short: >
    Take logged context_features as the point-in-time vector x. Recompute
    only to check we did not cheat.
  process:
    - title: Prefer the logged snapshot
      detail: >
        Stage 1 of the online service already stored x_raw at decision time.
        That is the gold copy. We turn those fields into a numeric vector
        with a fixed column order.
    - title: Fill holes with old defaults, not new ones
      detail: >
        If a feature was missing then, we impute the segment default that
        existed then — not today’s default. A new feature that cannot be
        backfilled is dropped for that training window.
    - title: Hunt for leakage
      detail: >
        If a recomputed “as-of” value disagrees with the log, we flag the
        row. Future timestamps or TTL violations are the usual culprits.
        A high mismatch rate means stop training and fix the feature job.
  try: Run after join. Leakage should be ~0 because this demo trains on the logged snapshot.

- id: ol_causal
  number: 4
  title: Causal training
  tagline: Fit E[reward | person, price] for the online scorer.
  about: >
    This is the model the online service calls in Stage 4. We fit how
    reward changes with the discount, after correcting for the fact that
    the old policy already preferred some arms. The default recipe is a
    DR-learner: an outcome model plus an inverse-propensity correction.
  in_short: >
    On uncensored, non-degraded rows, fit μ(x, a) with cross-fitting, then
    a treatment-effect model τ(x) versus list price.
  process:
    - title: Build the matrices
      detail: >
        X is the point-in-time feature vector. A is the arm we actually
        showed. Y is the reward. P is the logged propensity. Degraded and
        censored rows stay out. Arms with too few samples are dropped or
        merged so we do not fit noise.
    - title: Fit an outcome model
      detail: >
        A ridge S-learner predicts reward from [features + one-hot arm].
        We cross-fit: train on one half, predict the other, so the next
        step does not use a model that already memorized the same row.
    - title: Build the DR pseudo-outcome
      detail: >
        For each arm versus list price we form μ(target) − μ(baseline) +
        (Y − μ(chosen)) / propensity. If either the outcome model or the
        propensity is roughly right, this estimate of uplift is honest.
    - title: Fit τ and package the artifact
      detail: >
        A second ridge model predicts that pseudo-outcome from X. We store
        model_id, arm list, coefficients, R², and sample counts. That file
        is what OPE and the registry will judge.
  try: Train DR-learner, then S-learner. Compare R² and per-arm τ. Raise min samples to drop rare arms.

- id: ol_bandit
  number: 5
  title: Bandit update
  tagline: Refresh how eagerly we explore each discount.
  about: >
    Online Thompson sampling carries a posterior per arm (θ, A⁻¹). The
    streaming update is fast and noisy. The nightly job rebuilds those
    posteriors from the full weighted history so one unlucky day does not
    dominate.
  in_short: >
    For each arm, solve a weighted ridge regression of reward on x, with
    weights 1 / propensity, and store θ and the effective sample size.
  process:
    - title: Gather the history for each arm
      detail: >
        Rows are split by the arm that was actually shown. An arm we never
        explored keeps a prior (identity matrix) so it still has a chance
        tomorrow.
    - title: Weight by inverse propensity
      detail: >
        Rarely chosen arms are up-weighted. That counters the old policy’s
        taste. A ridge term keeps the matrix invertible when two features
        move together.
    - title: Write posteriors the online service can load
      detail: >
        θ̂ = A⁻¹ b is the new mean. Effective sample size tells us whether
        an arm is still in “explore” (high σ) or “mature” (low σ). Drift
        can reset σ when the world changes.
  try: Run after causal training. Check effective_sample_size per arm — tiny ESS means that arm is still under-explored.

- id: ol_ope
  number: 6
  title: OPE evaluation
  tagline: Estimate a new policy’s value without putting it in front of shoppers.
  about: >
    Off-policy evaluation is the reason we logged propensity. We ask:
    “If we had used the candidate policy on last week’s traffic, what
    reward would we have earned?” If the answer is not clearly better —
    with a confidence interval and enough effective samples — the model
    does not ship.
  in_short: >
    Score the candidate with IPS, SNIPS, DM, or DR (default). Bootstrap a
    95% CI. Reject if ESS is too small or arms do not overlap the log.
  process:
    - title: Define logging vs candidate
      detail: >
        π₀ is the old policy (logged propensity). π₁ is the candidate:
        exploit (always take the new model’s best arm) or ε-greedy. The
        importance weight is π₁(x, a) / π₀(x, a) on the arm we actually
        showed.
    - title: Run several estimators
      detail: >
        IPS is unbiased and noisy. SNIPS shrinks that noise. DM uses only
        the outcome model and can be biased. DR mixes them and is unbiased
        if either piece is right. That is why DR is the default gate input.
    - title: Check the diagnostics
      detail: >
        Effective sample size must be at least 10% of N. Max weight ≤ 100.
        Every arm the candidate loves must have appeared in the logs.
        Fail any of those and we do not trust the number — we extend the
        data window instead of guessing.
  try: Compare estimator=dr vs ips, and candidate=exploit vs logging. Logging should land near the mean observed reward.

- id: ol_registry
  number: 7
  title: Model registry
  tagline: Remember what we trained, on which data, with which scores.
  about: >
    A pickle on a laptop is not a production model. The registry (MLflow
    in production, a JSON file here) stores the artifact, its metrics,
    and its lineage: data hash, reward definition, OPE report, code
    version. No lineage, no promotion.
  in_short: >
    Register the causal + bandit artifacts as Staging. Promotion to
    Production is the gate’s job, not a human copying files.
  process:
    - title: Write the bundle
      detail: >
        One record holds model_id, type, coefficients, bandit posteriors,
        and the latest OPE report. Duplicate ids are versioned rather than
        overwritten.
    - title: Attach lineage
      detail: >
        Training window, sample count, and metric snapshot travel with the
        file. If those fields are missing, the gate must refuse. We need
        to answer “what data made this model?” a month from now.
    - title: Move through stages
      detail: >
        None → Staging (training succeeded) → Production (OPE + canary
        succeeded) → Archived (superseded). Rollback is “point traffic at
        the previous Production record”.
  try: Run after OPE. You should see a new Staging record. The gate tab decides whether it becomes Production.

- id: ol_gate
  number: 8
  title: Deployment gate
  tagline: Only ship if it is better, sure, fair, and fast.
  about: >
    Training success is not a deploy. The gate is a checklist: OPE value
    above current, confidence interval clears the current value, ESS is
    healthy, fairness gap is small, p99 latency still fits the budget,
    schema still matches. Fail any box and we keep the live model.
  in_short: >
    all(checks) → promote and start shadow/canary. Otherwise stay on
    current. Live regressions auto-rollback.
  process:
    - title: Score the checklist
      detail: >
        OPE better, OPE significant (CI lower bound > current), ESS ratio
        ≥ 0.1, fairness gap < 5%, latency p99 < 100ms, schema compatible.
        A tie keeps the current model. An inconclusive CI means “get more
        days of log”, not “ship and hope”.
    - title: Climb the rollout ladder
      detail: >
        Shadow (log only) → 1% canary → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%. Each step
        watches live margin, conversion, errors, and fairness against a
        holdout. This lab stops at the decision and shows the planned
        ladder.
    - title: Arm the rollback
      detail: >
        If live reward drops more than 5%, p99 exceeds 150ms, errors
        exceed 1%, fairness breaks, or propensity drift (PSI) exceeds
        0.25, traffic snaps back to the previous Production artifact.
  try: Run the gate on a freshly registered model. If OPE is not clearly better, you will see keep_current and the failing check.

- id: ol_reward
  number: null
  title: Reward modeler
  tagline: Pin what Y means for this training window.
  about: >
    Revenue, margin, LTV-proxy, and composite are different questions.
    This job recomputes Y under one definition and stores the contract
    so causal training and OPE cannot silently mix rewards.
  in_short: Re-label the training table with one pinned reward definition.
  process:
    - title: Choose the definition
      detail: Margin is default. Revenue ignores cost. LTV down-weights churn. Composite blends them.
    - title: Rewrite Y
      detail: Every labeled row gets the new reward. Degraded rows stay excluded.
  try: Switch to revenue and compare mean_reward to the margin run.

- id: ol_fairness
  number: null
  title: Fairness parity
  tagline: Watch price gaps across segments — not as model features.
  about: >
    Protected or sensitive groupings are logged for audit and never fed
    to the scorer. If average price diverges more than 5% across
    segments, the deployment gate should fail.
  in_short: Compare mean price and reward by segment. Flag a gap ≥ 5%.
  process:
    - title: Group the backfill table
      detail: Segment is the demo grouping. Production would use a separately stored audit attribute.
    - title: Measure the gap
      detail: (max mean price − min mean price) / midpoint. Under 0.05 passes.
  try: Run after backfill. Inspect group_price_mean for guest vs VIP.

- id: ol_drift
  number: null
  title: Drift (PSI)
  tagline: Did the world move under the model?
  about: >
    Population Stability Index on features and propensity, older half vs
    newer half. PSI ≥ 0.2 means stop and retrain or widen exploration.
    Logging-broken systems should disable exploration entirely.
  in_short: PSI per feature plus propensity. drift_ok if max PSI < 0.2.
  process:
    - title: Split the log in time
      detail: First half is expected. Second half is actual.
    - title: Histogram and PSI
      detail: Sum (actual − expected) × log(actual / expected) per bin.
  try: Needs ≥ 16 backfill rows. Seed 80 decisions first.

- id: ol_rollout
  number: null
  title: Rollout
  tagline: Shadow → canary → ramp, with a kill switch.
  about: >
    A Production artifact does not go to 100% traffic. Shadow logs only.
    Canary 1% then 5%, then 25/50/100. A reward drop > 5%, p99 > 150ms,
    or error rate > 1% snaps back to shadow.
  in_short: Advance the ladder or force a rollback. Serving swaps RegistryScorer into the cache.
  process:
    - title: Advance one step
      detail: shadow → canary_1 → canary_5 → ramp_25 → ramp_50 → full_100.
    - title: Watch live KPIs
      detail: Simulate a drop with reward_drop to see auto-rollback.
  try: Promote via the gate first. Then advance. Set reward_drop to 0.08 to roll back.

===== FILE: configs/segments.yaml =====
guest:
  bandit: cold-start prior, wide exploration
  causal: average elasticity
  guardrail: heavy caps, no personalization without consent
new:
  bandit: explore plus a light exploit
  causal: uplift of first purchase
  guardrail: onboarding discount cap
returning:
  bandit: contextual Thompson sampling
  causal: price sensitivity by RFM
  guardrail: margin floor + MAP
vip:
  bandit: exploit, small explore
  causal: retention vs margin
  guardrail: never below MAP; silent badge
at_risk:
  bandit: explore win-back arms
  causal: reactivation uplift
  guardrail: time-limited offers; MAP still binds


===== FILE: configs/stages.yaml =====
- id: board
  number: null
  title: Price board
  tagline: See what each customer is offered on each product.
  about: >
    This page is not one pipeline stage. It is the finished result of every
    stage working together. Think of it as the storefront view: six shoppers
    walk up to five products, and each person can be shown a different price
    because their history, consent, and risk look different.
  in_short: >
    Run the full pricing pipeline once for every customer × product pair,
    then put the offers on one grid so you can compare them.
  process:
    - title: Gather the people and the products
      detail: >
        The service loads the public customer profiles (Maya, James, Priya,
        Alex, Noah, and a guest) and the SKU catalog (earbuds, headphones,
        case, cable, locked speaker). Each profile already carries a segment,
        consent flag, and behavioral history. Each SKU already carries list
        price, cost, MAP, stock, and whether it may be discounted.
    - title: Price every pairing the same way
      detail: >
        For each customer and each SKU the service runs stages 0 through 8.
        It uses exploit mode, which means “pick the arm the model likes most”
        rather than randomly exploring. That keeps the grid stable so you are
        comparing context, not coin flips.
    - title: Show list price next to the offer
      detail: >
        Each cell is the customer-facing price after guardrails, scoring, and
        rounding. If a cell says “list price”, the pipeline decided (or was
        forced) not to discount. Click a cell to open the arms and scores
        behind that one decision.
    - title: Read across a row or down a column
      detail: >
        A row is one person facing five products. A column is one product
        facing six people. That is the point of contextual pricing: the same
        earbuds can be $44.99 for Maya and $50 for Alex, because Alex opted
        out of personalization.
  try: Click a cell, or a profile then a SKU, to inspect one full decision.

- id: ingestion
  number: 0
  title: Request ingestion
  tagline: Accept the request only if it is complete and safe to run.
  about: >
    Every pricing call starts here. The storefront sends a small JSON payload
    (“who is shopping, which SKU, on which device”). Stage 0 does not pick a
    price. It decides whether the rest of the pipeline is allowed to start,
    and it freezes the rulebook that this request will use.
  in_short: >
    Check the form, give the decision a unique ID, stamp the time, and lock
    the model versions so they cannot change mid-flight.
  process:
    - title: Check that the request makes sense
      detail: >
        Required fields must be present and have the right types. The SKU is
        mandatory because we cannot price “nothing”. Cart value cannot be
        negative. If the payload is broken, the service stops with HTTP 400
        and never builds a half-finished context. A bad request must not leak
        into the model.
    - title: Give the decision a unique, time-ordered ID
      detail: >
        A new decision_id (UUID v7) is created unless the caller already sent
        one. Time-ordered IDs make logs easy to sort. This ID is what support,
        analytics, and later “did they buy?” events will join on. If you send
        the same decision_id twice, the service returns the first answer
        instead of pricing again. That is idempotency: retries do not create
        a second coupon or a second experiment assignment.
    - title: Trust the server clock, keep the client clock
      detail: >
        Phones can have the wrong time. Campaign windows and coupon expiry
        must use the server’s clock. The time the app claimed is stored next
        to it for debugging, but it does not drive the decision.
    - title: Pin the versions for this request
      detail: >
        Right now the service writes down which policy, causal model,
        guardrail pack, and price ladder it will use (for example ts_v7,
        s_learner_v1, gr_v12). If someone hot-reloads a new model one
        millisecond later, this request still finishes on the old pins. That
        prevents a torn decision where guardrails came from v12 and scores
        came from v13.
    - title: Look up the product
      detail: >
        The SKU is loaded from the catalog (list price, cost, MAP, stock,
        discountable flag). Unknown SKU → HTTP 404. We do not invent a price
        for a product we do not sell.
    - title: Treat a missing customer as a guest
      detail: >
        No login is not an error. The shopper becomes segment “guest”. Later
        stages will refuse personalization and usually serve list price. That
        is safer than guessing who they are.
  try: Leave SKU blank for a 400. Type a fake SKU for a 404. Run once, paste the decision_id, run again — you should see an idempotent cache hit.

- id: preprocess
  number: 1
  title: Preprocessing
  tagline: Turn “who is this person?” into numbers the model can read.
  about: >
    The model cannot read a name or a cookie. It needs a clean vector of
    features, called x. Stage 1 builds that vector from identity, the online
    feature store, and the current request. It also enforces privacy: if the
    shopper did not consent to personalization, their history is wiped from x
    before any model sees it.
  in_short: >
    Find the person, fetch their recent behavior, fill gaps, hide PII, and
    encode everything into a standard numeric vector.
  process:
    - title: Resolve who the shopper is
      detail: >
        A logged-in customer_id wins over an anonymous cookie or device id.
        Maya maps to the “returning” profile with two past orders. An unknown
        id is treated as a new / cold-start customer. No id at all is a guest.
        If two identities conflict, the logged-in account is trusted.
    - title: Fetch live features
      detail: >
        The service asks the online feature store (Redis in production, a
        local snapshot here) for things like sessions in the last 7 days,
        lifetime orders, predicted LTV, and price sensitivity. These are the
        same features the model was trained on. If the store is down, we do
        not crash — we fall back to segment defaults and mark the decision
        “degraded” so it will not be used as training data.
    - title: Fill holes and clip extremes
      detail: >
        Every feature has a time-to-live. A stale “sessions_7d” is replaced
        with the typical value for that segment (returning vs VIP vs guest).
        A missing value gets a global default. A wild outlier (5,000 page
        views in a week) is clipped into a sane range and flagged. The model
        should see familiar numbers, not garbage.
    - title: Respect consent and strip private data
      detail: >
        If consent.personalization is false — or missing — behavioral fields
        (orders, LTV, sensitivity, age band, and so on) are replaced with
        generic defaults. Email, phone, and name are dropped entirely. The
        model is then scoring “a typical shopper in this segment”, not Alex
        Rivera the person. That is why Alex often sees list price even though
        he looks like a returning customer.
    - title: Encode into the vector x
      detail: >
        Numbers are standardized with the mean and standard deviation from
        training data — we never recompute those on the live request, or the
        model would drift. Categories such as segment, geo, channel, and
        device become one-hot columns (returning = 1, vip = 0, …). A
        “was this missing?” column travels with each number so the model can
        tell “zero orders” from “we do not know”.
    - title: Hash the vector
      detail: >
        A SHA-256 of x is stored as x_hash. Logs can say “this was the exact
        context” without reprinting a huge array, and a score cache can key
        on (x_hash, arm set, model version).
  try: Switch from Maya to Alex (consent off) and watch price_sensitivity_score snap back to the generic 0.5. Toggle “feature store down” to see missing flags and degraded=true.

- id: guardrails
  number: 2
  title: Guardrails
  tagline: Cross off any discount the business is not allowed to give.
  about: >
    A model will happily recommend a 30% off if that looks profitable on
    paper. Guardrails are the adult in the room. They are hard rules — legal,
    financial, fairness, and safety — and they override the model. This stage
    does not choose the winner. It only decides which prices are still legal
    to consider.
  in_short: >
    Start from a discount ladder, delete any arm that breaks a rule, and keep
    list price as the last resort.
  process:
    - title: Start from the discounts we might offer
      detail: >
        Each segment has a ladder of discount percentages. Returning shoppers
        might see 0%, 5%, 10%, 15%. VIP is narrower. At-risk is deeper. Each
        step is an “arm” with an id like disc_10, meaning 10% off the list
        price. Guardrails will now keep or drop those arms.
    - title: Apply the static (always-on) rules
      detail: >
        Price floor — the price must stay above cost × (1 + minimum margin).
        If earbuds cost $28 and min margin is 15%, we cannot go below $32.20.
        Price ceiling — never above MSRP. MAP — never below the manufacturer’s
        advertised price (earbuds MAP is $44.99, so 15% off $50 is illegal).
        If the SKU is marked “not discountable”, every discount arm dies and
        only list price remains. Outside a campaign window, same result.
    - title: Apply the dynamic (this-moment) rules
      detail: >
        These depend on the shopper and the stock right now. Frequency cap —
        do not hand another coupon if they already used too many in 30 days.
        Inventory — if stock is under the safety threshold (10 units here),
        do not discount a scarce item. Competitor band — do not wander more
        than 10% from the competitor’s price. Bot score — refuse discounts to
        likely scrapers. Consent — no personalized discount without consent.
        Fairness — VIP should not receive a deeper cut than policy allows.
    - title: When rules disagree, use a priority order
      detail: >
        Legal constraints (MAP, consent, abuse) beat fairness, which beats
        margin, which beats frequency, which beats operational convenience.
        We never “average” two conflicting rules. The stricter legal one wins.
    - title: Write down what survived
      detail: >
        The output is a list of allowed arms, a list of blocked arms each
        with a reason code (margin_floor, below_map, low_inventory, …), and a
        small constraint summary the causal model can see. If every discount
        is blocked, list price is still allowed. Checkout never goes blank.
    - title: If the rule service is down
      detail: >
        Use the last cached ruleset. If there is no cache either, fail safe
        and offer only list price. Making money with a broken rule engine is
        worse than making no promotional margin for a few minutes.
  try: Raise min margin to 0.80 — most arms die with margin_floor. Set stock to 5 — discounts die with low_inventory. Force consent off — personalized discounts disappear.

- id: candidates
  number: 3
  title: Candidate generation
  tagline: Build the short menu of prices the model is allowed to choose from.
  about: >
    After guardrails, we still need a concrete list of prices: $50, $47.50,
    $45.00, …. That list is the action space A(x). It must be small enough
    to learn from, deterministic for the same shopper, and overlapping with
    the prices we have used before so we can later say “would a new policy
    have been better?”
  in_short: >
    Take the segment’s discount ladder, keep only the arms guardrails allowed,
    and attach a real dollar price and margin to each one.
  process:
    - title: Pick the right ladder for this person
      detail: >
        Guest, new, returning, VIP, and at-risk each have their own set of
        discounts. Priya (at-risk) starts with deeper cuts (15–30%) because
        the business is willing to spend more to keep her. James (VIP) starts
        with shallower cuts — we do not want to train a loyal customer to
        wait for a sale.
    - title: Widen the ladder for high-margin products
      detail: >
        If a SKU has a lot of room between cost and list price (the leather
        case is a good example), extra rungs from the default ladder are
        merged in. Low-margin goods stay tight so we do not accidentally
        give away the profit.
    - title: Keep only legal, unique prices
      detail: >
        Drop any arm guardrails already blocked. Drop anything above MSRP.
        If two arms round to the same dollar amount, keep one. The result
        should be about 5–20 arms: enough to learn, few enough to score
        quickly.
    - title: Attach money to each arm
      detail: >
        For 10% off a $50 list price the arm becomes {id: disc_10, price:
        45.00, discount: 0.10, margin: 37.8%}. These are the options stage 4
        will score and stage 5 will pick from. The ladder version (cs_v3) is
        logged so we know which menu was on the table.
    - title: Never return an empty menu
      detail: >
        If filtering removed everything, we put list price back and mark
        no_arms. A shopper always sees a number. That number might just be
        “full price”.
  try: Run Maya, then Priya, then James on the same SKU. Priya’s deeper ladder often collapses to list price on earbuds because 15% off is below MAP.

- id: causal
  number: 4
  title: Causal scoring
  tagline: Guess how much each remaining price would earn, and how unsure we are.
  about: >
    Now we have a few legal prices. For each one we ask: “If we show this
    price to this shopper, what reward should we expect?” Reward here is not
    “did they like it?” — it is a business outcome. The default is expected
    margin: (price − cost) × chance they buy. We also keep an uncertainty
    number so the next stage knows when to explore.
  in_short: >
    Score every surviving arm with an expected reward μ and a spread σ,
    using the shopper’s features and the size of the discount.
  process:
    - title: Agree on the reward we are optimizing
      detail: >
        This request is pinned to one definition (margin, revenue, LTV-proxy,
        or a blend). We do not mix them. “Highest revenue” and “highest
        margin” will pick different discounts — a cheap sale can grow
        revenue and destroy profit. The lab lets you switch the definition
        to see that tension.
    - title: Estimate the chance of a purchase
      detail: >
        A simple S-learner (one model that sees both the person and the
        discount) predicts conversion. A price-sensitive shopper gets more
        lift from 10% off than a VIP does. High churn slightly lowers the
        baseline. In production you can drop in a stronger causal model
        (DR-learner, Dragonnet) without changing this stage’s inputs/outputs.
    - title: Turn conversion into expected reward
      detail: >
        Expected margin ≈ (price − cost) × P(buy). Expected revenue ≈ price ×
        P(buy). A deeper discount can raise P(buy) and still lower margin if
        the extra purchases do not cover the giveaway. μ is that expected
        dollar amount. Uplift is μ minus the list-price μ — “how much better
        than doing nothing.”
    - title: Say how unsure we are
      detail: >
        σ is the uncertainty. Deep discounts we have rarely shown, and
        brand-new customers, get a larger σ. The bandit uses that as an
        exploration bonus: “we are not sure, so maybe try it.” We also store
        a 10th and 90th percentile so you can see a pessimistic / optimistic
        range, not just a point guess.
    - title: Score every arm in one batch
      detail: >
        All remaining arms go through the model together (budget about 30ms).
        If the model times out, we reuse a cached score or a wide “we have
        no idea” prior and mark the decision degraded. We still need numbers
        so the bandit can pick something.
  try: Raise price sensitivity — discount arms’ μ should rise relative to list price. Toggle causal timeout to see the wide fallback prior.

- id: bandit
  number: 5
  title: Bandit selection
  tagline: Pick one price, sometimes to earn, sometimes to learn.
  about: >
    If we always chose the arm with the highest μ, we would never learn
    whether a less-used discount is actually better. A bandit balances
    exploitation (take the current best) and exploration (try something
    uncertain). Whatever it picks, it must write down the probability that
    this arm was going to win — the propensity. Without that number we cannot
    later evaluate a new policy on old logs.
  in_short: >
    Draw a possible reward for each arm, take the highest draw, and record
    how likely that arm was to win.
  process:
    - title: Combine two kinds of uncertainty
      detail: >
        The causal model already gave us σ (“the world is noisy”). The
        bandit adds its own posterior uncertainty (“we have not tried this
        arm on people like you very often”). New customers and new arms get
        extra spread so they get sampled more. Total uncertainty is the two
        combined.
    - title: Thompson sampling — one imaginary outcome each
      detail: >
        For every arm we draw one random number from a bell curve centered
        on μ. The arm with the luckiest draw wins this request. Arms with
        high μ win often. Arms with high σ win sometimes, which is how
        exploration happens naturally. If you run this tab in “live” mode
        several times, the winner should jitter.
    - title: Force a little extra exploration
      detail: >
        On top of sampling, about 5% of requests pick a uniformly random
        legal arm (ε-greedy). Every 20th request is also forced to explore.
        That guarantees we keep collecting data even if the model becomes
        overconfident.
    - title: Compute the propensity
      detail: >
        Propensity is P(this arm would be chosen | this context). With two
        arms there is a closed-form formula. With more, we simulate the
        contest about 256 times and count wins. If the number would be 0 we
        clamp it to 0.05. A zero propensity makes later math (divide by
        propensity) explode, so we never allow it.
    - title: Exploit mode for the board
      detail: >
        The price board uses exploit mode: skip the random draw and take the
        arm with the highest μ. That is “what the model currently believes is
        best.” Use live mode on this tab when you want to see exploration.
        The shopper never sees the propensity; only the log does.
  try: Set mode to live and click Run several times — the chosen arm should change. Switch to exploit — it should stick to the highest μ.

- id: postprocess
  number: 6
  title: Post-processing
  tagline: Dress the chosen price for a human, without changing the policy.
  about: >
    The bandit picked an arm, say disc_10 at $45.00. Shoppers do not want a
    raw arm id. They want $44.99, a “10% off” badge, and a coupon that
    expires in ten minutes. This stage is presentation. It must not sneak
    around guardrails, and it must not put model guts on the page.
  in_short: >
    Round the price, issue a coupon if needed, write the badge and the
    support reason codes, and set an expiry time.
  process:
    - title: Start from the chosen arm’s price
      detail: >
        If the arm is disc_10 on a $50 item, we begin at $45.00. Everything
        after this is cosmetic or operational (coupons, copy), not a new
        pricing decision.
    - title: Charm-round, but never break the floor
      detail: >
        People expect $39.99 more than $40.00. If charm rounding would push
        the price under the margin floor (or MAP), we bump it back up. Making
        a price look pretty is not an excuse to sell below cost.
    - title: Bind a short-lived coupon
      detail: >
        Any real discount gets a coupon code (SAVE10-…) with a short TTL,
        default 10 minutes, so the offer cannot be screenshotted and reused
        next month. If the coupon service is down we still return the price
        and skip the code. Checkout > coupons.
    - title: Decide what the shopper sees
      detail: >
        A badge (“10% off”) is shown only when the discount is at least 5%.
        VIP shoppers do not get a badge — the cheaper price is applied
        quietly so we do not train them to hunt sales. Reason codes such as
        segment:returning and arm:disc_10 go to customer support and legal,
        not as marketing copy.
    - title: Stamp when the offer dies
      detail: >
        expires_at tells the storefront how long it may cache this price.
        After that, they must ask again. The world (stock, campaign, model)
        may have changed.
  try: Uncheck charm pricing and compare $45.00 vs $44.99. Break the coupon service — you still get a price, with coupon_skip.

- id: logging
  number: 7
  title: Logging
  tagline: Write down exactly what we knew, what we showed, and why.
  about: >
    A price without a log is a one-off. With a log we can audit a complaint,
    train the next causal model, and — most importantly — evaluate a new
    policy on old traffic without running a risky A/B test first. That last
    part is called off-policy evaluation (OPE). It only works if we stored
    the propensity and the full set of arms we could have chosen.
  in_short: >
    Save the experience tuple (who, what we could offer, what we did offer,
    how likely that was, which models) without delaying the shopper.
  process:
    - title: Assemble the experience tuple
      detail: >
        One record per decision: decision_id, timestamp, customer and session,
        the human-readable features (x_raw), the hash of x, which arms were
        on the table, which arm was chosen, the final price, the propensity,
        whether this was an exploration draw, every version pin, guardrail
        reason codes, and how many milliseconds each stage took.
    - title: Why propensity is not optional
      detail: >
        Next month you may want to ship a new bandit. OPE answers “would that
        new policy have made more margin on last week’s traffic?” The
        estimators (IPS, DR) reweight old decisions by 1 / propensity. If we
        forgot to log it, or logged a zero, the math fails and you are stuck
        running a live experiment on real customers.
    - title: Deliver the log without blocking checkout
      detail: >
        The record is appended to a local file now (data/log_buffer). In
        production it goes to Kafka topic pricing.decisions.v1, keyed by
        decision_id. If Kafka is down we buffer on disk and keep serving
        prices. The shopper must never wait on a logger.
    - title: Join the outcome later
      detail: >
        Minutes or days later a purchase, refund, or “left without buying”
        event arrives with the same decision_id. We attach revenue, margin,
        and units. That completed row (context, action, propensity, reward)
        is what trains the next model. Rows marked degraded or
        exclude_from_training are kept for audit but skipped for learning,
        so a fallback day does not teach the model “always use list price”.
  try: Change the customer or SKU and inspect the JSON. Confirm propensity is there and exclude_from_training matches degraded.

- id: response
  number: 8
  title: Response building
  tagline: Send the storefront a price — and nothing it should not see.
  about: >
    The internal decision is rich: scores, propensities, model ids, traces.
    The client needs almost none of that. Stage 8 is a privacy and
    competitive-safety filter. If a competitor or a curious browser user
    views the network tab, they should learn the price, not how we think.
  in_short: >
    Copy the customer-facing fields into a small JSON document and leave
    the science in the log.
  process:
    - title: Keep only what the app must render
      detail: >
        The public body is price, currency, discount percent, optional badge,
        optional coupon, a short list of reason codes, decision_id (so
        support can find the log), and expires_at (so the app knows when to
        ask again).
    - title: Hide the scoring machinery
      detail: >
        Propensity, μ, σ, sampled scores, causal_model_id, policy hash, and
        the full feature vector stay out of the response. Support can still
        look them up server-side with the decision_id. This tab shows both
        payloads side by side so the difference is obvious.
    - title: Be tidy under failure
      detail: >
        Optional fields that are empty are omitted, not sent as null. If
        something goes wrong while formatting JSON we fall back to a tiny
        {price, currency, decision_id} so the page still draws a number.
  try: Compare the two JSON cards. Left = browser/app. Right = internal only.

- id: fallback
  number: 9
  title: Fallback handling
  tagline: If something breaks, still show a price — a safe one.
  about: >
    Checkout cannot display “error computing discount”. Stage 9 is a ladder
    of increasingly conservative backups. Each step down is less smart and
    more safe. We always tell the log that we degraded, and we keep those
    rows out of training so a bad afternoon does not become the next model’s
    idea of normal.
  in_short: >
    Walk from “full intelligence” down to “just the catalog price” until
    something works, then return that price with a reason.
  process:
    - title: Prefer the full pipeline
      detail: >
        If every dependency is healthy, we do nothing special. The normal
        stages already produced a price.
    - title: Then reuse cached model scores
      detail: >
        If the causal model is slow or down, reuse the last scores for this
        (context, arm set, model version). Better a slightly stale μ than a
        blank page. Flag causal_timeout.
    - title: Then use segment defaults
      detail: >
        If the feature store is down we already built x from “typical
        returning shopper” (or guest) values. Pricing continues, but it is
        not personalized. Flag degraded_features.
    - title: Then pick a random legal arm
      detail: >
        If the bandit itself throws, we ε-greedy over the arms guardrails
        still allow. We lose the clever explore/exploit math but we do not
        lose a price. Flag bandit_fallback.
    - title: Then serve list price
      detail: >
        If guardrails conflict or no arms remain, the shelf price in the
        catalog is the answer. No coupon, no badge. Flag no_arms or
        guardrail_all_blocked.
    - title: Last resort — static catalog
      detail: >
        If even the catalog lookup is unhappy, return whatever static price
        we have and a minimal JSON body. Ugly, but the cart still works.
        Flag static_catalog.
    - title: Coupon and logger must not take the site down
      detail: >
        A dead coupon service skips the code. A dead Kafka buffers locally.
        Those are inconveniences, not checkout outages.
  try: Tick the failure boxes one at a time, then several at once. You should always get a dollar amount, with degraded=true and a readable reason.

- id: cache
  number: 10
  title: Model cache & hot reload
  tagline: Keep the brains in memory, and swap them without dropping requests.
  about: >
    Loading a model from disk on every request would blow the 69ms budget.
    Stage 10 keeps the causal model, bandit state, guardrail rules, and
    ladders in RAM. When data science publishes a new file, we swap the
    pointer. Requests that already started keep the versions they pinned in
    stage 0, so a reload cannot split one decision across two models.
  in_short: >
    Serve from memory, reload by swapping a pointer, and leave in-flight
    requests on the old pointer.
  process:
    - title: What lives in memory
      detail: >
        Causal model (ONNX in production, the S-learner here), bandit
        posteriors, the current guardrail JSON, price ladders, and segment
        default features. Hits are microseconds, not disk I/O.
    - title: How a reload works
      detail: >
        A config push or registry webhook says “gr_v13 is ready”. We load the
        new artifact beside the old one, check it is not corrupt, then swing
        the pointer. New requests pin v13. Requests already in preprocess
        still hold v12 on their DecisionContext.
    - title: What we refuse to do
      detail: >
        We do not apply a half-written file. We do not change versions on a
        request that already pinned them. If the new file is bad we keep the
        old one and alert. If two versions disagree in a way we cannot
        reconcile, we reject the swap.
    - title: Memory pressure
      detail: >
        If too many old models pile up, unused ones are evicted (least
        recently used). The currently pinned production set is never evicted.
        This demo only needs one set, so eviction is not wired.
  try: Click Reload configs. The version chips at the top refresh from the YAML files without restarting the server. In-flight decisions would keep their old pins.

  title: PDP personalized price
  channel: web
  trigger: Shopper opens a product page
  reward: purchase or add-to-cart

  channel: email

  reward: purchase within 24h
  risk: Frequency cap (max 1 / 30 days)
  defaults: {customer_id: c_maya, sku: SKU-1234, mode: live}

  channel: email
  trigger: At-risk / churned segment
  reward: reactivation purchase
  risk: Only send if OPE uplift is positive
  defaults: {customer_id: c_priya, sku: SKU-CASE, mode: exploit}

  channel: web
  trigger: Multi-item cart
  reward: basket margin
  risk: Margin floor on the bundle, not each SKU
  defaults: {customer_id: c_maya, sku: SKU-CASE, cart_value: 79, mode: exploit}

  channel: app

  risk: Churn vs ARPU tradeoff
  defaults: {customer_id: c_james, sku: SKU-VIP, mode: exploit}

  channel: partners
  trigger: Account requests a quote
