  risk: Sales approval / floor; MAP
  defaults: {customer_id: c_james, sku: SKU-LOCKED, mode: exploit}

  channel: web

  risk: Re-explore after the prior shifts
  defaults: {customer_id: c_maya, sku: SKU-LOW, mode: live}

  channel: web

  reward: click-through then purchase
  risk: Mismatched grid vs PDP kills conversion
  defaults: {customer_id: c_maya, sku: SKU-1234, sticky: true, mode: exploit}
- id: uc12_campaign
  title: Batch campaign scoring
  channel: email
  trigger: CRM list scored overnight
  reward: purchase inside the offer TTL
  risk: Same propensity contract as the hot path
  defaults: {customer_id: c_maya, sku: SKU-1234, channel: email, mode: exploit}
  batch:
    - {customer_id: c_maya, sku: SKU-1234, channel: email, mode: exploit}
    - {customer_id: c_priya, sku: SKU-CASE, channel: email, mode: exploit}
    - {customer_id: c_james, sku: SKU-VIP, channel: email, mode: exploit}
- id: uc13_killswitch
  title: Kill switch / merchandiser freeze
  channel: web
  trigger: SRE or legal flips control plane
  reward: none — serve list price
  risk: Must take effect on the next request
  defaults: {customer_id: c_maya, sku: SKU-1234, mode: live}
- id: uc14_sticky
  title: Cross-channel sticky price
  channel: web
  trigger: Same shopper opens mobile after desktop
  reward: cart completion
  risk: Price flip inside the TTL looks unfair
  defaults: {customer_id: c_maya, sku: SKU-1234, sticky: true, mode: live}

  title: Daily discount budget exhausted
  channel: web
  trigger: Promotional spend hits the cap
  reward: protect margin
  risk: Exploration must stop; list price only
  defaults: {customer_id: c_maya, sku: SKU-1234, mode: live}

<body>
  <header>
    <div class="brand">
      <h1>Personalized Pricing System — Azure implementation</h1>
      <p>Canada Central · a readable runbook, with commands where you need them</p>
    </div>
    <div class="progress">Done <b id="doneCount">0</b> / <span id="totalCount">0</span></div>
  </header>
  <div class="layout">
    <nav class="toc" id="toc"></nav>
    <article>

<section class="card" id="kids">
  <p class="phase">Overview</p>
  <h2>What this project is, and what Azure adds</h2>
  <p>The Pricing Decision Service answers a single operational question: given this shopper, this SKU, and this moment, what price should we show, and how do we learn from that choice later? That question is already implemented in this repository. A request is ingested, identity and features are resolved, guardrails drop illegal prices, a causal model scores what remains, a bandit selects an arm, a coupon is bound, the decision is logged with a propensity, and the client receives only a safe JSON body. Azure does not rewrite that sequence. It is the production platform around it: a place to run the process, remember features, store catalog and coupons, carry logs, train overnight, and freeze discounts without a new build.</p>
  <p>On your laptop the same stages run in FastAPI with a YAML catalog, an in-memory feature store, and JSONL files. In Azure those adapters point at managed services in Canada Central so personal data stays in Canada. A public channel still calls <code>POST /v1/price</code>. Front Door terminates TLS and filters bots; API Management authenticates and rate-limits, and it keeps internal routes such as <code>/v1/price:explain</code> off the internet. Container Apps runs this FastAPI app with a p99 target under 100 ms. During that call the service reads online features from Redis and catalog or identity from Cosmos DB, applies guardrails, scores arms, picks one, and writes a redeemable offer. The shopper sees a price, a badge, a coupon, reason codes, and a <code>decision_id</code>. Propensity and model identifiers never leave on that response.</p>
  <p>After the response, Event Hubs records the experience tuple of context, action, propensity, and versions without blocking checkout. A later purchase or refund is posted to the outcomes hub keyed by the same <code>decision_id</code>. Capture lands in ADLS. Offline jobs join those streams, reconstruct point-in-time features, train, and run off-policy evaluation. Azure ML registers a candidate only if that estimate beats the current policy and the fairness and drift gates pass. A new Container Apps revision is then opened in shadow, given a slice of traffic, and either ramped or rolled back. App Configuration can force list price on the next request if legal or merchandising needs an immediate freeze. App Insights is what tells you the new revision is slow or incomplete so you can send traffic back to the last good one.</p>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="kids-story" /><span>I understand Azure hosts this PDS; it does not replace the causal or bandit code.</span></label>
</section>

<section class="card" id="components">
  <p class="phase">Bill of materials</p>
  <h2>All Azure components for this project</h2>
  <p>You do not provision this list on day one. You grow it in the same order the system itself depends on: a place to run, then a way to change rules and hide secrets, then the two stores on the hot path, then a log that never lies about propensity, then overnight training, and only then a public door. Every database, cache, and log that holds shopper or decision data is created in Canada Central. When you connect these services, you change adapters under <code>services/</code>. You do not rewrite the causal model or the bandit.</p>
  <h3>Foundation</h3>
  <p>Start with a dedicated development subscription and the Entra directory that comes with it. That subscription is the billing and permission root; production pricing data should never live in a personal account. Sign in with <code>az login</code> and confirm you have Contributor. People use Entra to open the portal and the CLI; the Container App later uses a managed identity in the same directory so GitHub never holds a long-lived client secret. Create one resource group in Canada Central and put everything for this environment inside it, because deleting that group is how you stop paying. On the same day, set a Cost Management budget that emails you at a modest cap. A budget warns; it does not always shut resources off. Finally create a single Log Analytics workspace for the environment. Container Apps, App Insights, and later APIM should all write there. Several workspaces make simple questions impossible to ask.</p>
  <h3>Hosting</h3>
  <p>Azure Container Registry is the private shelf for Docker images of this app. Names are globally unique. Basic SKU is enough in development; production can move to Standard or Premium and, later, a replica in Canada East. A Container Apps environment is the cluster those images join, and you attach Log Analytics when you create it. The Container App itself is this FastAPI process: stages 0 through 10, a small CPU and memory footprint at first, replicas when traffic grows, and revisions so a new policy can take one percent of calls without replacing the old one. In development ingress can be external so you can open a browser; in production it should be internal behind API Management, and <code>/v1/price:explain</code>, <code>/v1/control</code>, and admin reload must never be on the public product. A Container Apps Job is the same codebase on a schedule for campaign lists. Do not fire thousands of single HTTP calls from Logic Apps with no backpressure. Do not begin on AKS or App Service. Container Apps is the host until you have a platform team and a scale problem that revisions cannot solve.</p>
  <h3>Config and secrets</h3>
  <p>Give the Container App a system-assigned managed identity and grant that identity roles, rather than baking Cosmos or Redis keys into environment variables. Key Vault holds the remaining secrets: Redis URL, Event Hubs send string, App Insights connection string, Cosmos key until you switch the SDK to Entra. Use RBAC on the vault, not a mix of access policies. App Configuration is the live rulebook that used to be <code>control_plane.yaml</code> and <code>versions.yaml</code>: kill switch, merchandiser freeze, policy and model pins, daily discount budget. Those flags must refresh in seconds. If App Configuration cannot be read, fail closed to list price using a cache no older than a minute. Free SKU is fine in development; production wants Standard and a replica in Canada East.</p>
  <h3>Online data plane</h3>
  <p>Two stores sit on the request. Redis, on TLS port 6380, is the millisecond cache that replaces the in-memory feature store and sticky-price map. Keys are short-lived: features, a sticky offer for shopper and SKU, frequency caps, and an incremented discount budget. If Redis is unavailable you still return a price from coarser defaults, because checkout cannot wait. Basic C0 is enough to learn the adapter; production should be Premium, zone redundant, and private. Cosmos DB is the system of record that replaces <code>catalog.yaml</code>, identity profiles, the coupon list, and decision lookup. Use separate containers partitioned on sku, customer_id, offer code, and customer_id again for decisions. Serverless is the right development SKU. Production should autoscale, back up, and fail over to Canada East. A coupon in Cosmos is a promise: a later policy change must not void a code already shown.</p>
  <h3>Streaming and lakehouse</h3>
  <p>Decision logs are telemetry, not a command queue, which is why Event Hubs with Kafka enabled replaces the JSONL buffer and Service Bus does not. One hub, <code>pricing.decisions.v1</code>, receives every <code>decide()</code> with propensity, policy id, candidate-set version, and experiment variant. Another, <code>pricing.outcomes.v1</code>, receives purchase, refund, and return keyed by <code>decision_id</code>, joined later on a seven-day window net of refunds. Joining only on customer_id will mix people and ruin OPE. Schema Registry versions that JSON so a silent field drop cannot poison training. ADLS Gen2 with hierarchical namespace is the lake: bronze for raw capture, silver for joined point-in-time rows, gold for OPE and campaigns. A plain blob account without HNS will fight Spark. Event Hubs Capture writes bronze on a timer so you do not need a custom consumer on day one. Keep capture in the same region. If the hub is down, buffer locally and stop exploring until it returns, or the propensities you log will be fiction.</p>
  <h3>Machine learning</h3>
  <p>Training never runs inside the online Container App. Azure ML is the workspace that replaces <code>data/registry/models.json</code> and laptop jobs: you submit causal, bandit, and OPE work, keep lineage, and register a model only when OPE beats the current policy and fairness and drift are acceptable. Serverless compute is enough for the numpy learners in this repo. A GPU cluster is a later choice and a common way to leave money running overnight. When joins no longer fit a single node, Microsoft Fabric or Azure Databricks in Canada Central reads the same ADLS paths that <code>offline/join.py</code> and <code>backfill.py</code> use today. The standing risk is training on “current” features instead of the values as of the decision timestamp.</p>
  <h3>Public edge</h3>
  <p>Skip Front Door and API Management until a real channel is calling you. Then Front Door Premium is the anycast door with TLS, bot manager, origin health, and a Canada POP. Point it at APIM or the app, never at the explain endpoint. Put the WAF in Detection for a week, then Prevention, with an allowlist for partner IPs. API Management is the product split that used to live in <code>gateway.py</code>: public price, checkout outcomes, CS lookup, and an internal product for explain and control. Developer SKU has no SLA; production should be Standard v2 or Premium on a VNet.</p>
  <h3>Observability and rollback</h3>
  <p>A bandit you cannot measure is just random prices. Application Insights, created against the same Log Analytics workspace, replaces in-process counters for production: duration of <code>/v1/price</code>, calls out to Redis and Cosmos, exceptions. Do not log propensity or PII in custom events; <code>decision_id</code> is enough on the public path. Metric alerts and an action group with a named owner fire on slow p99, 5xx, a gap between requests and Event Hub ingress, a stale kill switch, or a fairness gap. A workbook later fills the role of the lab Monitor tab: reward versus predicted value, propensity PSI, segment price gaps, logging completeness. Sampled telemetry makes those charts lie.</p>
  <h3>Security and Canada</h3>
  <p>In production, Redis, Cosmos, Key Vault, Storage, and Event Hubs should not have public endpoints. A VNet, private endpoints, and Container Apps integration are required, and DNS must be in place or the app will hang on names. Purview scans ADLS, classifies PII, and is how you show PIPEDA evidence that bronze decisions are not a free-for-all. Protected attributes used for audit must never enter the feature vector. Defender for Cloud watches for a public Cosmos account, Redis without TLS, and vulnerable images in ACR. Do not ship an image the registry has already flagged.</p>
  <h3>CI/CD</h3>
  <p>GitHub Actions with Entra OIDC is how a commit becomes a revision: tests, image, push to ACR, Container Apps update. Failed pytest must not deploy. Do not put <code>AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET</code> in GitHub. Federate the app registration and use <code>azure/login</code> with the federated token.</p>
  <h3>What to leave alone</h3>
  <p>AKS is a later host if Container Apps and a platform team cannot meet a sustained ten thousand decisions a second with a mesh you truly need. App Service slots are not a substitute for a propensity-logged canary. Service Bus is fine for occasional commands, not for this telemetry. Azure Communication Services is optional if you have no email provider; even then, never send a price that is not already in the offer ledger.</p>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="all-components" /><span>I have read this as a sequence, not a shopping cart, and I will not start on AKS or Service Bus.</span></label>
</section>

<section class="card" id="picture">
  <p class="phase">Architecture</p>
  <h2>How the pieces sit together</h2>
  <p>A shopper on web, app, email, or a till never talks to Python directly. The call arrives at Front Door, which is the public door: TLS, geography, and a WAF that should absorb bots so the bandit does not waste exploration on scrapers. API Management sits behind that door and decides who may ask for a price. The product that channels use exposes <code>POST /v1/price</code> and nothing that leaks scores. Explain, control, and admin stay on an internal product.</p>
  <p>The work itself runs on Container Apps. Azure Container Registry holds the Docker image of this repo; the app is a replica of that image, scaled out if the line gets long, and versioned as revisions so you can send one percent of traffic to a new policy without replacing the old one. While a request is in flight, App Configuration is the live rulebook for kill switch, freeze, and version pins, and Key Vault is where connection strings live. The process authenticates to both with a managed identity rather than a password in an environment variable.</p>
  <p>Two stores are on the hot path. Redis is the desk cache: feature vectors, a sticky price for the same shopper and SKU, frequency caps, and a running discount budget, all with TTLs measured in seconds or minutes. If Redis is down you still answer, using coarser defaults, because checkout cannot wait. Cosmos DB is the cabinet of record: list price, MAP, cost, stock, the identity graph and consent flag, the coupon ledger that must still redeem after a policy change, and the decision row a CS agent looks up by <code>decision_id</code>.</p>
  <p>Once a price has been returned, logging must not sit on the critical path. Event Hubs, with Kafka enabled so the existing topic design still makes sense, carries <code>pricing.decisions.v1</code> and <code>pricing.outcomes.v1</code>. Every decision event includes propensity and the version pins; without that, off-policy evaluation later is guesswork. Capture writes those events into ADLS Gen2 as bronze files. Nightly jobs turn bronze into silver training rows with point-in-time features, then gold OPE reports. Azure Machine Learning is where those jobs run and where a model is registered only if OPE, fairness, and drift agree. App Insights watches latency and completeness so a bad revision can be given zero traffic. All of that data plane stays in Canada Central; Canada East is for disaster recovery, not for cheaper training.</p>
  <div class="diagram">This repo                              Azure
--------------------------            --------------------------------
FastAPI :8080                    →    Container Apps
gateway.py                       →    Front Door + APIM
feature_store.py                 →    Redis
catalog.yaml + identity          →    Cosmos DB
control_plane.yaml               →    App Configuration
coupon / sticky                  →    Cosmos offers + Redis TTL
decisions.jsonl                  →    Event Hubs
data/lake/*.jsonl                →    ADLS Gen2
offline/pipeline.py              →    Azure ML jobs
models.json                      →    Azure ML registry
metrics.py                       →    App Insights</div>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="kids-picture" /><span>I can explain the online path and the overnight path in a few sentences.</span></label>
</section>

<section class="card" id="tools">
  <p class="phase">Tools</p>
  <h2>The tools you actually touch</h2>
  <p>On the laptop you only install two clients. Azure CLI is the remote control; almost every create and update in this runbook is an <code>az</code> command, and you start with <code>az login</code> so Azure knows which subscription to bill. PowerShell is the window you paste those commands into on this Windows machine. Docker packages the Python app as an image so Container Apps is not installing packages by hand; <code>docker build</code> and <code>docker push</code> are the two verbs that matter.</p>
  <p>In the subscription, a resource group is the folder for an environment. Create everything inside <code>rg-pds-canadacentral-dev</code> (or whatever name you printed) and you can delete that folder to stop paying. ACR is the private registry that stores <code>pds-api</code> tags. Container Apps is the process host: replicas for load, revisions for canary. Log Analytics is the shared diary those replicas write to. Key Vault holds Redis, Cosmos, and Event Hubs credentials. App Configuration holds the kill switch and version pins that must change without a new image.</p>
  <p>Redis is the millisecond cache for features and sticky prices. Cosmos DB is the document store for catalog, identity, and the offer ledger. Event Hubs is the stream that must see every decision with a propensity. ADLS Gen2 is the lake those streams become. Azure ML is where training and OPE run, and where a model is allowed into the registry. App Insights is the stopwatch and the alarm. Front Door and API Management are the public edge; skip them until a real channel is calling you, then put them in front so explain and control never face the internet.</p>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="kids-tools" /><span><code>az version</code> works and Docker Desktop is running.</span></label>

  <h3>The same work, written out</h3>
  <p>Sign in to the subscription that will be billed.</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>az login
az account show --query "{name:name, id:id}" -o table</code></pre>

  <p>Set names once. Canada Central keeps data in Canada. ACR names must be globally unique, so a random suffix is appended.</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>$Location = "canadacentral"
$EnvName  = "dev"
$Prefix   = "pds"
$Suffix   = Get-Random -Minimum 1000 -Maximum 9999
$RG       = "rg-$Prefix-$Location-$EnvName"
$ACR      = ($Prefix + "acr" + $EnvName + $Suffix).ToLower()
$ACA_ENV  = "cae-$Prefix-$EnvName"
$APP      = "ca-$Prefix-api"
$LA       = "log-$Prefix-$EnvName"
Write-Host "RG=$RG  ACR=$ACR"</code></pre>

  <p>Create the resource group — one container for every later resource, and the thing you delete when you want charges to stop.</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>az group create --name $RG --location $Location</code></pre>

  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>az provider register --namespace Microsoft.App
az provider register --namespace Microsoft.ContainerRegistry
az provider register --namespace Microsoft.OperationalInsights</code></pre>

  <p>Build and run locally so the image is known-good before Azure sees it.</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>docker build -t pds-api:local .
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 pds-api:local</code></pre>
  <p>Open <code>http://127.0.0.1:8080</code>, then stop the container with Ctrl+C.</p>

  <p>Create the registry and push that image. ACR names are globally unique; the suffix from earlier is what makes yours available.</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>az acr create -g $RG -n $ACR --sku Basic --admin-enabled true
az acr login -n $ACR
docker tag pds-api:local "$ACR.azurecr.io/pds-api:v0.1.0"
docker push "$ACR.azurecr.io/pds-api:v0.1.0"</code></pre>

  <p>Create logs, the Container Apps environment, and the app. Attach Log Analytics when you create the environment so you are not hunting for a diary later.</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>az monitor log-analytics workspace create -g $RG -n $LA -l $Location
$WS_ID  = az monitor log-analytics workspace show -g $RG -n $LA --query customerId -o tsv
$WS_KEY = az monitor log-analytics workspace get-shared-keys -g $RG -n $LA --query primarySharedKey -o tsv

az containerapp env create -n $ACA_ENV -g $RG -l $Location --logs-workspace-id $WS_ID --logs-workspace-key $WS_KEY

az containerapp create `
  --name $APP -g $RG --environment $ACA_ENV `
  --image "$ACR.azurecr.io/pds-api:v0.1.0" `
  --registry-server "$ACR.azurecr.io" `
  --target-port 8080 --ingress external `
  --cpu 0.5 --memory 1.0Gi `
  --min-replicas 1 --max-replicas 3 `
  --env-vars PDS_ENV=azure-dev PDS_HOST=0.0.0.0 PDS_PORT=8080

$FQDN = az containerapp show -g $RG -n $APP --query properties.configuration.ingress.fqdn -o tsv
Write-Host "OPEN https://$FQDN/"</code></pre>

  <p>Verify health and a price call. You should see <code>"status":"ok"</code> and a JSON body with <code>price</code> and <code>decision_id</code>.</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>curl "https://$FQDN/health"
curl -s -X POST "https://$FQDN/v1/price" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"customer_id\":\"c_maya\",\"sku\":\"SKU-1234\",\"cart_value\":50,\"mode\":\"exploit\"}"</code></pre>

  <p>Add Key Vault and App Configuration so a kill switch can take effect without a new image.</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>$KV = "kv-pds-dev-$Suffix"
$APPCS = "appcs-pds-dev-$Suffix"
az keyvault create -n $KV -g $RG -l $Location

az appconfig feature set -n $APPCS --feature pds.kill_switch --description "Serve list price only"</code></pre>

  <p>When you want charges to stop, delete the resource group. That removes everything you created inside it.</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>az group delete --name $RG --yes --no-wait</code></pre>

  <h2>1. What this project becomes on Azure</h2>
  <p>Every local piece has one production home. Keep this picture in mind while you build; it is the target, not a catalog of extras. A shopper on web, app, email, a till, or a partner never talks to Python. The call arrives at Front Door, which terminates TLS, picks a Canada POP, and should absorb bots so the bandit does not waste exploration on scrapers. Sticky dicts and coupon lists become Redis TTLs plus a Cosmos ledger so an issued price is still honored. In-process metrics become App Insights. The lab UI stays the same app, on internal ingress only, because <code>/v1/price:explain</code> must not face the internet.</p>

<section class="card" id="login">

  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>az keyvault create -n $KV -g $RG -l $Location --enable-rbac-authorization true

<section class="card" id="redis">
  <p class="phase">Phase 5</p>
  <h2>7. Redis — online features + sticky prices</h2>
  <p>This replaces <code>FeatureStore</code> and <code>StickyPriceStore</code>. A feature GET should finish in well under two milliseconds. Create the cache with TLS only, then put the connection string in Key Vault rather than on the Container App as a raw environment secret.</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>az redis create -g $RG -n $REDIS -l $Location --sku Basic --vm-size C0 --enable-non-ssl-port false
$REDIS_HOST = az redis show -g $RG -n $REDIS --query hostName -o tsv
$REDIS_KEY  = az redis list-keys -g $RG -n $REDIS --query primaryKey -o tsv
az keyvault secret set --vault-name $KV --name redis-connection `
  --value "rediss://:$REDIS_KEY@$REDIS_HOST:6380/0"</code></pre>
  <p>Keys are short-lived and named so you can find them in a hurry. Feature vectors live at <code>feat:{customer_id}</code> with the TTL from <code>features.yaml</code>, often five minutes. A sticky offer is <code>sticky:{customer_id}:{sku}</code> for about thirty minutes. How often this shopper has already been discounted is <code>freq:{customer_id}:disc:30d</code>. The daily discount budget is an incrementing <code>budget:discount:yyyy-mm-dd</code> that expires after two days. In <code>services/feature_store.py</code> and <code>services/control_plane.py</code>, swap the in-memory dict for <code>redis.Redis.from_url(os.environ["REDIS_URL"])</code> and keep the same methods (<code>get</code>, <code>lookup</code>, <code>remember</code>) so <code>orchestrator.py</code> does not change.</p>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="p5-redis" /><span>Two <code>POST /v1/price</code> with <code>"sticky": true</code> for Maya + SKU-1234 return the same price. Redis Browser / <code>redis-cli GET sticky:c_maya:SKU-1234</code> shows the key.</span></label>
</section>

<section class="card" id="cosmos">
  <p class="phase">Phase 6</p>
  <h2>8. Cosmos DB — catalog, identity, offer ledger, CS lookup</h2>
  <p>Cosmos is the cabinet of record that replaces <code>catalog.yaml</code>, the identity dict, the coupon list, and CS lookup. Create a serverless account in Canada Central with session consistency, then four containers in a database named <code>pricing</code>: catalog partitioned on <code>sku</code>, customers and decisions on <code>customer_id</code>, offers on <code>code</code>. Put the URI and key in Key Vault. A coupon written here is a promise — a later policy change must not void a code already shown.</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>az cosmosdb create -g $RG -n $COSMOS --locations regionName=$Location failoverPriority=0 isZoneRedundant=false --default-consistency-level Session --capabilities EnableServerless
az cosmosdb sql database create -g $RG -a $COSMOS -n pricing
az cosmosdb sql container create -g $RG -a $COSMOS -d pricing -n catalog --partition-key-path "/sku"
az cosmosdb sql container create -g $RG -a $COSMOS -d pricing -n customers --partition-key-path "/customer_id"
az cosmosdb sql container create -g $RG -a $COSMOS -d pricing -n offers --partition-key-path "/code"
az cosmosdb sql container create -g $RG -a $COSMOS -d pricing -n decisions --partition-key-path "/customer_id"

$COSMOS_URI = az cosmosdb show -g $RG -n $COSMOS --query documentEndpoint -o tsv
$COSMOS_KEY = az cosmosdb keys list -g $RG -n $COSMOS --query primaryMasterKey -o tsv
az keyvault secret set --vault-name $KV --name cosmos-uri --value $COSMOS_URI
az keyvault secret set --vault-name $KV --name cosmos-key --value $COSMOS_KEY</code></pre>
  <h3>Load the demo catalog once</h3>
  <p>Write a one-off script <code>scripts/load_cosmos.py</code> that reads <code>configs/catalog.yaml</code> and upserts each SKU and customer. Run it from your laptop with the Key Vault secrets after <code>az login</code>. A catalog document carries list price, cost, MAP, stock, and whether the SKU is discountable. A customer document carries segment, consent, features, and geo band. An offer document is the redeemable code plus expiry and the <code>decision_id</code> that created it. A decision document is what CS looks up: price, propensity, timestamp, and reason codes. Replace <code>CatalogService.get</code>, <code>IdentityService.resolve</code>, <code>CouponService.issue/lookup/redeem</code>, and <code>lookup_decision</code> with Cosmos reads. Unknown SKU is still 404. Guest still works with no <code>customer_id</code>.</p>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="p6-cosmos" /><span>After loading YAML, <code>GET /v1/catalog</code> on the Azure FQDN returns Maya, James, Priya, Alex, Noah + 5 SKUs. Issue a coupon, <code>GET /v1/offers/{code}</code>, redeem once, second redeem is 400.</span></label>
</section>

<section class="card" id="events">
  <p class="phase">Phase 7</p>
  <h2>9. Event Hubs + ADLS — the experience tuple must never block checkout</h2>
  <p>Today <code>DecisionLogger</code> writes JSONL. Production: emit to Event Hubs using the Kafka protocol (so the existing “Kafka topic” mental model stays). Capture lands in the lake automatically.</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>az eventhubs namespace create -g $RG -n $EHNS -l $Location --sku Standard --enable-kafka true --capacity 1
az eventhubs eventhub create -g $RG --namespace-name $EHNS -n pricing.decisions.v1 --message-retention 7 --partition-count 8
az eventhubs eventhub create -g $RG --namespace-name $EHNS -n pricing.outcomes.v1 --message-retention 7 --partition-count 4

az storage account create -g $RG -n $STG -l $Location --sku Standard_LRS --kind StorageV2 --enable-hierarchical-namespace true
az storage fs create -n lake --account-name $STG
az storage fs directory create -n bronze/decisions --file-system lake --account-name $STG
az storage fs directory create -n bronze/outcomes --file-system lake --account-name $STG
az storage fs directory create -n silver/training --file-system lake --account-name $STG
az storage fs directory create -n gold/ope --file-system lake --account-name $STG

# Capture decisions → ADLS (no extra consumer required for bronze)
$STG_ID = az storage account show -g $RG -n $STG --query id -o tsv
az eventhubs eventhub update -g $RG --namespace-name $EHNS -n pricing.decisions.v1 `
  --enable-capture true --capture-interval 300 --capture-size-limit 314572800 `
  --destination-name EventHubArchive.AzureBlockBlob `
  --storage-account-resource-id $STG_ID `
  --blob-container lake --archive-name-format "bronze/decisions/{Namespace}/{EventHub}/{PartitionId}/{Year}/{Month}/{Day}/{Hour}/{Minute}/{Second}"</code></pre>
  <p>Store the Event Hubs connection string in Key Vault as <code>eventhub-send</code>. In <code>services/logger.py</code> turn Kafka on and produce to <code>$EHNS.servicebus.windows.net:9093</code> with SASL_SSL. The payload is the same experience dict <code>build_experience()</code> already builds, and it must carry <code>decision_id</code>, <code>context_hash</code>, chosen arm, propensity, policy and causal model ids, candidate-set version, variant, sticky replay, and whether training should ignore the row. If Event Hubs is down, buffer locally (you already have <code>log_buffer</code>), mark the decision degraded, and disable exploration until the bus is healthy — otherwise off-policy evaluation is fiction.</p>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="p7-eh" /><span>POST a price, then check Event Hubs metrics (incoming messages = 1) and, within 5 minutes, a capture blob under <code>bronze/decisions/</code>.</span></label>
  <p>Outcomes use the existing API, but persist to the second hub:</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>POST /v1/outcomes
{
  "decision_id": "&lt;from price response&gt;",
  "event_type": "purchase",
  "revenue": 44.99,
  "margin": 16.99,
  "units": 1
}</code></pre>
</section>

<section class="card" id="ml">
  <p class="phase">Phase 8</p>
  <h2>10. Offline learning on Azure ML + Spark</h2>
  <p>Do not train on the Container App. Nightly jobs map one-for-one onto <code>offline/pipeline.py</code>. Ingest turns Event Hub capture into Delta bronze on ADLS. Join matches decisions to outcomes on <code>decision_id</code> with a seven-day reward window net of refunds, and writes silver training rows. Backfill reconstructs features as of the decision timestamp, not “current.” Causal training is an Azure ML job (the numpy S-learner in this repo first, EconML later). The bandit job writes a policy artifact. OPE computes IPS, SNIPS, DR, a bootstrap interval, and effective sample size into <code>gold/ope</code>. The registry step registers a model only if the DR estimate of the new policy beats the current one by the threshold, ESS is healthy, the fairness gap is under five percent, and max PSI is under 0.2. The gate then opens a new Container Apps revision at zero traffic — shadow — before any shopper sees it.</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>az extension add -n ml
az ml workspace create -g $RG -n $MLW -l $Location --storage-account $STG

# First training job: reuse the Python you already have
# Create a job YAML (save as infra/train-causal.yml) then:
# az ml job create -g $RG -w $MLW -f infra/train-causal.yml</code></pre>
  <p>A minimal <code>infra/train-causal.yml</code> reuses the pipeline you already run locally:</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>$schema: https://azuremlschemas.azureedge.net/latest/commandJob.schema.json
command: python -c "from pricing_decision.offline.pipeline import OfflinePipeline; from pricing_decision.orchestrator import PricingOrchestrator; OfflinePipeline(PricingOrchestrator()).run('ol_ope', {'seed_n': 200})"
experiment_name: pds-offline
environment:
  image: mcr.microsoft.com/azureml/openmpi4.1.0-ubuntu20.04
  conda_file: ../conda.train.yml
compute: azureml:serverless
outputs:
  model:
    type: uri_folder</code></pre>
  <p>When a candidate clears the gate, copy a revision at zero percent, then move a percent, then five, twenty-five, and a hundred. If an App Insights alert fires, put the new revision back to zero. That is the same shadow-then-canary story as the lab, expressed as Container Apps traffic weights.</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code># New revision, 0% traffic = shadow (logs, does not serve)
az containerapp revision copy -g $RG -n $APP --from-revision &lt;current&gt; --image "$ACR.azurecr.io/pds-api:v0.2.0"
az containerapp ingress traffic set -g $RG -n $APP --revision-weight &lt;old&gt;=100 &lt;new&gt;=0

# Canary
az containerapp ingress traffic set -g $RG -n $APP --revision-weight &lt;old&gt;=99 &lt;new&gt;=1
# then 5, 25, 100. Auto-rollback: if App Insights alert fires, set new=0.</code></pre>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="p8-ml" /><span>One Azure ML job completes, a model appears in the registry tagged <code>policy_id</code> + <code>causal_model_id</code>, and OPE JSON is in <code>gold/ope/</code>.</span></label>
</section>

<section class="card" id="edge">
  <p class="phase">Phase 9</p>
  <h2>11. Front Door + APIM (public edge)</h2>
  <p>Do this when a real channel will call pricing. Until then, the Container Apps hostname plus an IP restriction is enough. When you do put a door in front, split products the way <code>gateway.py</code> already thinks. Channels call <code>POST /v1/price</code> with a JWT or subscription key, about fifty requests per second per customer, and they never receive an explain body. CRM and email call <code>POST /v1/price:batch</code> with a managed identity and a larger payload limit. Checkout posts outcomes with a managed identity. CS tools look up <code>GET /v1/decisions/{id}</code> with Entra and a CS group. Explain, control, and admin are not on Front Door at all; they live on an internal APIM product.</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code># APIM is billed even when idle. Use Developer SKU in dev, Standard v2 in prod.
az apim create -g $RG -n "apim-$Prefix-$EnvName-$Suffix" -l $Location --sku-name Developer --publisher-email you@company.com --publisher-name "Pricing"

# Front Door Premium: WAF bot manager + Canada anycast
# Portal is easier the first time: Create profile → origin group = APIM gateway hostname
# WAF: Bot manager + rate limit + geo allow CA/US if that is your market</code></pre>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="p9-edge" /><span>Public <code>POST /v1/price</code> works with a subscription key. <code>/v1/price:explain</code> from the internet returns 404/401.</span></label>

<section class="card" id="monitor">
  <p class="phase">Phase 10</p>
  <h2>12. Monitor, fairness, rollback</h2>
  <p>A bandit you cannot measure is just random prices. Create Application Insights against the same Log Analytics workspace you attached to Container Apps, then pass the connection string into the app. Instrument FastAPI with OpenTelemetry toward Azure Monitor. You can keep the in-process Prometheus counters for the lab, but App Insights is what production paging will use.</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>az monitor app-insights component create -g $RG -l $Location -a $AI --workspace $LA
$AI_CONN = az monitor app-insights component show -g $RG -a $AI --query connectionString -o tsv
az containerapp update -g $RG -n $APP --set-env-vars "APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING=$AI_CONN"</code></pre>
  <p>Before you take the bandit live, those alerts have to exist with a named owner. If p99 of <code>/v1/price</code> sits above 100 ms for five minutes, page on-call and scale replicas. If availability drops under 99.9 percent or 5xx crosses one percent, put all traffic on the last known-good revision. If Event Hub ingress lags request count by more than a tenth of a percent, force exploit so you stop exploring into an incomplete log. If rolling hourly revenue falls far below predicted value, freeze discounts and investigate. If propensity PSI crosses 0.2, stop exploring and retrain. If a protected-group price gap exceeds five percent, turn the kill switch on. If the kill switch flag cannot be read, fail closed to list price.</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code># Example: 5xx → rollback traffic (fill IDs after first revision)
az monitor metrics alert create -g $RG -n pds-5xx `
  --scopes $(az containerapp show -g $RG -n $APP --query id -o tsv) `
  --condition "avg Requests > 0" `
  --description "Replace condition with Http5xx when the metric namespace is visible" `
  --action $(az monitor action-group create -g $RG -n ag-pds-oncall --short-name pds --action email you you@company.com --query id -o tsv)</code></pre>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="p10-mon" /><span>App Insights live metrics show POST /v1/price. You have an action group email. You documented the revision rollback command in your on-call notes.</span></label>
</section>

<section class="card" id="batch">
  <p class="phase">Phase 11</p>
  <h2>13. Batch campaigns (email / ads)</h2>
  <p>Do not loop HTTP from Logic Apps across thousands of customers with no backpressure. Use a Container Apps Job that calls the same <code>decide_batch()</code> path, logs propensities, and writes offer codes to Cosmos. Better still, a small worker that reads a customer list from ADLS, posts to <code>/v1/price:batch</code> in chunks of a hundred, and writes results to <code>gold/campaigns/</code>. The frequency cap still lives in Redis. Never email a price that is not already in the offer ledger.</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>az containerapp job create -g $RG -n job-pds-campaign --environment $ACA_ENV `
  --image "$ACR.azurecr.io/pds-api:v0.1.0" `
  --cpu 1 --memory 2Gi `
  --command "python" --args "-m" "pricing_decision.cli" "decide" "-f" "/input/campaign.json" `
  --trigger-type Manual</code></pre>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="p11-batch" /><span>A 50-row CSV of customer_id,sku produces 50 logged decisions with propensity and 50 Cosmos offer rows.</span></label>
</section>

<section class="card" id="code">
  <p class="phase">Code you must change</p>
  <h2>14. Adapter swap list (keep stage files)</h2>
  <p>Do not rewrite <code>stages/stage4_causal.py</code> or the bandit to “be Azure.” Swap adapters only. <code>config.py</code> grows settings for App Configuration, Redis, Cosmos, Kafka, and Key Vault. <code>services/feature_store.py</code> becomes Redis GET and SET of JSON. <code>services/control_plane.py</code> reads App Configuration flags, increments the Redis discount budget, and stores sticky prices. Catalog, identity, coupons, and decision lookup read Cosmos containers <code>catalog</code>, <code>customers</code>, <code>offers</code>, and <code>decisions</code>. <code>services/logger.py</code> produces to Event Hubs over Kafka and falls back to the local buffer. Outcomes go to <code>pricing.outcomes.v1</code>. The lake uses ADLS Delta. The registry uses the Azure ML SDK. Rollout talks to the Container Apps revision traffic API. <code>api/app.py</code> adds App Insights middleware and splits public routers from admin. Unit tests should still pass against in-memory fakes. Mark Azure integration tests so they skip unless <code>PDS_ENV</code> starts with <code>azure</code>.</p>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="p14-adapters" /><span>Unit tests still pass with in-memory fakes. Add integration tests marked <code>@pytest.mark.azure</code> that skip unless <code>PDS_ENV</code> starts with <code>azure</code>.</span></label>
</section>

<section class="card" id="privacy">
  <p class="phase">Phase 12</p>
  <h2>15. PIPEDA / Law 25 / fairness (Canada)</h2>
  <p>Every store that holds shopper or decision data is created in Canada Central. Confirm it with <code>az resource list -g $RG --query "[].{n:name,l:location}"</code> before you call this production. Consent already exists in preprocess: if the flag is off, the service sends a generic feature vector. Protected attributes such as exact age, gender, or ethnicity may live in a locked Cosmos container for audit and must never enter the feature vector; Azure Policy can deny unexpected columns in the training Delta table. In production, Key Vault and the data plane sit behind private endpoints, and public networks on Cosmos, Redis, and Storage are off. Retention in <code>control_plane.yaml</code> is 400 days; set Event Hub and ADLS lifecycle to match, then purge. Microsoft Purview scans ADLS, classifies PII, and is how you show that bronze decisions are not a free-for-all.</p>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="p12-privacy" /><span>Legal signed off: purpose of personalization, retention, kill switch, and “CS can explain a price by decision_id without model guts.”</span></label>
</section>

<section class="card" id="verify">
  <p class="phase">Go-live checks</p>
  <h2>16. Verification script (run against the Azure FQDN)</h2>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>$Base = "https://$FQDN"   # later: https://pricing.yourdomain.com
# 1 health
curl "$Base/health"
# 2 PDP exploit
curl -s -X POST "$Base/v1/price" -H "Content-Type: application/json" `
  -d '{"customer_id":"c_maya","sku":"SKU-1234","cart_value":50,"mode":"exploit"}'
# 3 holdout = list price
curl -s -X POST "$Base/v1/price:explain" -H "Content-Type: application/json" `
  -d '{"customer_id":"c_maya","sku":"SKU-1234","cart_value":50,"experiment_hint":"holdout"}'
# 4 kill switch
az appconfig feature enable -n $APPCS --feature pds.kill_switch
Start-Sleep 8
curl -s -X POST "$Base/v1/price" -H "Content-Type: application/json" `
  -d '{"customer_id":"c_maya","sku":"SKU-1234","cart_value":50}'
# expect 50.00
az appconfig feature disable -n $APPCS --feature pds.kill_switch
# 5 outcome join
# (use decision_id from step 2)
# 6 unknown SKU → 404
# 7 guest (no customer_id) → segment guest, no deep personalization
# 8 sticky two calls same price
# 9 budget: set spent = cap → list price
# 10 explain endpoint blocked from Front Door</code></pre>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="p16-verify" /><span>All 10 checks recorded in a wiki/PR. Holdout still returns only <code>disc_0</code>. Kill switch restored to off.</span></label>
</section>

<section class="card" id="cost">
  <p class="phase">Money</p>
  <h2>17. Cost sketch (Canada Central, 2026 ballpark)</h2>
  <p>These are order-of-magnitude numbers so you are not surprised on the invoice, not a quote from Microsoft. A development month of Container Apps, ACR, and Log Analytics is tens of dollars, Redis Basic another twenty, Cosmos serverless twenty to eighty, Event Hubs and ADLS thirty to sixty, and Azure ML jobs fifty to a hundred fifty if you remember to stop compute. Skip Front Door and APIM in development and the whole slice often lands between about 150 and 400 dollars a month. Production at serious traffic is a different conversation: hundreds for the app and logs, Redis Premium in the hundreds, Cosmos autoscale that can pass a thousand, Event Hubs and the lake a few hundred, ML and Spark from hundreds to a couple of thousand on a busy nightly, and APIM plus Front Door another thousand or two. At around ten thousand requests a second, plan on a few thousand to the high thousands a month, and put a named owner on the bill.</p>
  <p>Put a budget alert on the resource group on day one. A budget emails you; it does not always shut resources off.</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>az consumption budget create --budget-name pds-dev-cap --amount 400 --time-grain Monthly --category Cost --resource-group $RG --start-date (Get-Date -Format yyyy-MM-01)</code></pre>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="p17-budget" /><span>Budget + email alert created. You know who pays the bill.</span></label>
</section>

<section class="card" id="plan">
  <p class="phase">Calendar</p>
  <h2>18. Eight-week implementation plan</h2>
  <p>Week one is the lab on Container Apps and a GitHub Action that builds the image to ACR on every main push. Week two is Key Vault, the App Configuration kill switch, App Insights, and the split between public and admin routes. Week three is Redis: features, sticky prices, the frequency cap, and the discount budget. Week four is Cosmos: catalog, identity, the offer ledger, the YAML load, and CS lookup by <code>decision_id</code>.</p>
  <p>Week five is Event Hubs, ADLS capture, outcomes on the second hub, and a completeness dashboard. Week six is Spark join and backfill, the Azure ML causal and OPE job, the registry, and a shadow revision. Week seven is a one-percent canary with holdout still at ten percent of traffic so you can estimate causal effects, plus a fairness workbook. Week eight is Front Door and APIM, private endpoints, Purview, disaster recovery toward Canada East, and a game day with CS, legal, and merchandising: kill switch, Event Hub outage, Redis outage — and the service must still return a price.</p>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="p18-plan" /><span>Dates on a calendar. Week 8 game-day scheduled with CS + legal + merchandising.</span></label>
</section>

<section class="card" id="cicd">
  <p class="phase">CI/CD</p>
  <h2>19. GitHub Actions (build → ACR → Container Apps)</h2>
  <p>Create <code>.github/workflows/azure-deploy.yml</code> after you have an Azure AD app federated to GitHub (OIDC — no long-lived secrets):</p>
  <pre><button class="copy">Copy</button><code>name: deploy-pds
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      id-token: write
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: azure/login@v2
        with:
          client-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
          tenant-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
          subscription-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}
      - name: pytest
        run: pip install -e ".[dev]" && pytest
      - name: Build and push
        run: |
          az acr login -n ${{ secrets.ACR_NAME }}
          docker build -t ${{ secrets.ACR_NAME }}.azurecr.io/pds-api:${{ github.sha }} .
          docker push ${{ secrets.ACR_NAME }}.azurecr.io/pds-api:${{ github.sha }}
      - name: Deploy revision
        run: |
          az containerapp update -g ${{ secrets.RG }} -n ca-pds-api \
            --image ${{ secrets.ACR_NAME }}.azurecr.io/pds-api:${{ github.sha }}</code></pre>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="p19-cicd" /><span>A commit to main runs tests, pushes an image, and ACA shows a new revision. Failed pytest does not deploy.</span></label>
</section>

<section class="card" id="fallback">
  <p class="phase">Failure</p>
  <h2>20. Azure fallbacks (same ladder as the lab)</h2>
  <p>Checkout still needs a price when a dependency is sick, so the ladder is the same one you already coded, just aimed at Azure names. If Redis is down, serve a segment-level default feature vector, mark the call degraded, and still return a price. If Cosmos is down, use the catalog warmed into replica memory at boot; if that is cold, fall back to a static list price. If the causal model times out, reuse last scores in Redis, or the rule-based ladder. If Event Hubs is down, write the local buffer (or a blob) and switch to exploit only so you do not explore into a log you cannot keep. If App Configuration cannot be read, fail closed when the last known flag was kill, otherwise use cached flags no older than a minute. If APIM or Front Door is unhealthy, origin probes fail over to a second Container Apps environment in Canada East in production.</p>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="p20-fallback" /><span>Chaos: stop Redis in dev. <code>/v1/price</code> still 200 with a price and <code>degraded</code> on the explain endpoint.</span></label>
</section>

<section class="card" id="done">
  <p class="phase">Done when</p>
  <h2>21. Definition of done</h2>
  <p>You have implemented this project on Azure when a channel can <code>POST /v1/price</code> in Canada Central under a 100 ms p99 and receive only client fields, with no propensity on the wire; when every decision is in Event Hubs with propensity and version pins, and outcomes join within seven days; when kill switch, sticky TTL, and offer redeem work without a redeploy; when nightly OPE can block a bad model and a canary revision can roll back in one command; and when holdout traffic still exists so you can estimate causal effects, not only bandit regret.</p>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="done-1" /><span>A channel can <code>POST /v1/price</code> in Canada Central, p99 &lt; 100 ms, and get only client fields (no propensity).</span></label>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="done-2" /><span>Every decision is in Event Hubs with propensity + version pins; outcomes join within 7 days.</span></label>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="done-3" /><span>Kill switch, sticky TTL, and offer redeem work without a redeploy.</span></label>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="done-4" /><span>Nightly OPE can block a bad model; canary revisions can roll back in one command.</span></label>
  <label class="step"><input type="checkbox" data-k="done-5" /><span>Holdout traffic still exists so you can estimate causal effects, not only bandit regret.</span></label>
  <p>Start today with login, Docker, and Container Apps. Everything after that is swapping adapters. The pricing brain you already built stays the same. The files that support the first deploy are <code>Dockerfile</code>, <code>.dockerignore</code>, <code>infra/azure-up.ps1</code>, and this HTML runbook.</p>
</section>

<section class="card" id="overview">
  <p class="phase">Start here</p>
  <h2>How to read this</h2>
  <p>This repository is one product: a Pricing Decision Service that answers “what price should we show this shopper, for this SKU, right now?” and then learns from that choice overnight. The Python that does the work lives under <code>src/pricing_decision/</code>. The knobs that change without a code edit live under <code>configs/</code>. What the service writes while it runs lives under <code>data/</code>. The browser lab you are looking at is FastAPI serving <code>src/pricing_decision/web/index.html</code>. Azure does not add a second codebase; it is a runbook in <code>docs/</code> plus deploy scripts in <code>infra/</code> that host this same package.</p>
  <p>When you are lost, start at <code>src/pricing_decision/api/app.py</code>. That file is FastAPI. A live request hits <code>POST /v1/price</code>, which calls <code>PricingOrchestrator.decide()</code> in <code>orchestrator.py</code>, which walks stages 0 through 8. Overnight learning is the same orchestrator’s cousin, <code>offline/pipeline.py</code>, writing into <code>data/lake/</code>. To put the app on Azure you change adapters under <code>services/</code>, not the causal or bandit stages.</p>
  <p>Ignore generated folders. <code>.pytest_cache/</code> and <code>src/pricing_decision_service.egg-info/</code> appear after you install or test; they are not source. A local <code>.venv/</code> is your Python environment. None of those belong in the story of the product.</p>
</section>

<section class="card" id="tree">
  <p class="phase">At a glance</p>
  <h2>Folder tree</h2>
  <p>Everything important sits next to <code>pyproject.toml</code>. The package is src-layout, so imports are <code>pricing_decision....</code> and the installable name is <code>pricing-decision-service</code>.</p>
  <div class="diagram">Pricing/
  pyproject.toml          package name, deps, pytest, CLI entry
  README.md               how to install and call /v1/price
  Dockerfile              image Azure Container Apps will run
  .dockerignore
  .gitignore
  configs/                YAML the running service reads
  src/pricing_decision/   the Python package
    api/app.py            FastAPI  ← start here for HTTP
    web/index.html        this lab UI
    orchestrator.py       wires stages 0–10
    stages/               online pipeline
    services/             catalog, Redis-to-be, logger…
    core/                 request/response models
    offline/              lake, train, OPE, gate
    cli.py                pds serve / pds decide
  data/                   logs and lake files (generated)
  tests/                  pytest
  docs/                   Azure runbook + this map
  infra/                  PowerShell to deploy
  examples/               sample JSON request
  scripts/                one-off HTML helpers</div>
</section>

<section class="card" id="root">
  <p class="phase">Repo root</p>
  <h2>Root files</h2>
  <p><code>pyproject.toml</code> is how Python knows this is a package. It names the project <code>pricing-decision-service</code>, requires Python 3.11+, and lists FastAPI, uvicorn, pydantic, numpy, PyYAML, and prometheus-client. The optional <code>dev</code> extra adds pytest and httpx. The console script <code>pds</code> points at <code>pricing_decision.cli:main</code>. Setuptools is told to find packages under <code>src/</code>. Pytest is told to look in <code>tests/</code> with <code>src</code> on the path.</p>
  <p><code>README.md</code> is the human on-ramp: the stage table, a venv install, <code>pytest</code>, a one-shot <code>cli decide</code> against <code>examples/request.json</code>, and the HTTP verbs for serve mode. It is not the Azure runbook; that is <code>docs/azure-implementation.html</code>.</p>
  <p><code>Dockerfile</code> copies <code>pyproject.toml</code>, <code>README.md</code>, <code>src/</code>, <code>configs/</code>, and <code>examples/</code>, installs the package, and starts uvicorn on <code>pricing_decision.api.app:app</code> at port 8080. That is the same process you run on the laptop. <code>.dockerignore</code> keeps tests, data, and caches out of the image. <code>.gitignore</code> keeps venv, pyc, and data noise out of git.</p>
</section>

<section class="card" id="src">
  <p class="phase">Python</p>
  <h2>src / the package</h2>
  <p><code>src/pricing_decision/</code> is the only Python package you maintain. <code>__init__.py</code> exports the version string FastAPI shows on <code>/health</code>. Everything else is a role: <code>api</code> speaks HTTP, <code>web</code> is the lab page, <code>stages</code> is the online pipeline, <code>services</code> talks to catalog and logs, <code>core</code> holds shared types, <code>offline</code> is the night shift, and a handful of modules at the package root glue those together.</p>
  <p><code>config.py</code> is the compass. <code>ROOT</code> is the Pricing folder. <code>load_yaml("catalog.yaml")</code> always reads from <code>configs/</code>. <code>Settings</code> takes environment variables prefixed <code>PDS_</code> — host, port, whether Kafka is on, the log buffer directory, epsilon, the propensity floor. When you later point Redis or App Configuration at Azure, new settings land here, not in a stage file.</p>
</section>

<section class="card" id="api">
  <p class="phase">HTTP</p>
  <h2>FastAPI</h2>
  <p>The FastAPI application is <code>src/pricing_decision/api/app.py</code>. <code>create_app()</code> builds it; the module-level <code>app = create_app()</code> is what uvicorn loads. <code>api/__init__.py</code> re-exports <code>create_app</code> so tests can import it cleanly.</p>
  <p>The home page <code>GET /</code> returns <code>web/index.html</code>. <code>GET /azure</code> returns the Azure runbook. <code>GET /project</code> returns this file. <code>GET /health</code> is the liveness probe. The public pricing contract is <code>POST /v1/price</code>; the body that comes back has price, badge, coupon, reason codes, and <code>decision_id</code>, never propensity. <code>POST /v1/price:explain</code> is the internal twin that does leak scores, and it must stay off the public internet in production. Batch, outcomes, offer redeem, CS lookup, control plane, stage playground, offline run, architecture JSON, and admin reload are all routes on this same app.</p>
  <p>You start it with <code>python -m pricing_decision.cli serve</code>, or <code>python -m uvicorn pricing_decision.api.app:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --reload</code>. Open <code>http://127.0.0.1:8080/</code> for the lab. FastAPI’s own docs sit at <code>/docs</code> if you want the OpenAPI page.</p>
</section>

<section class="card" id="web">
  <p class="phase">Browser</p>
  <h2>Lab UI</h2>
  <p><code>src/pricing_decision/web/index.html</code> is the single-page lab. The four (now five) top buttons are pipelines: Project, Azure, Architecture, Online PDS, and Offline learning. Left-nav buttons under each pipeline are stages loaded from YAML through the API. Online and offline stages POST to <code>/v1/stages/run</code> and <code>/v1/offline/run</code>. Azure and Project are iframes of the HTML files in <code>docs/</code>. There is no React build; it is one HTML file with fetch calls.</p>
</section>

<section class="card" id="stages">
  <p class="phase">Hot path</p>
  <h2>Online stages</h2>
  <p><code>src/pricing_decision/stages/</code> is the checkout pipeline, one file per stage, numbered so the spec and the code stay aligned. <code>__init__.py</code> marks the folder as a package. You do not rewrite these files to “be Azure.”</p>
  <p><code>stage0_ingestion.py</code> validates the request, resolves the SKU in the catalog, and honors idempotency so a retried checkout does not mint a second decision. <code>stage1_preprocess.py</code> builds the feature vector: identity, consent, segment, and the raw <code>x</code> that later models see. If consent is off, the vector stays generic. <code>stage2_guardrails.py</code> drops illegal prices — MAP, floor, stock, frequency, budget — before anyone scores them. <code>stage3_candidates.py</code> turns what remains into a discrete arm ladder. Holdout collapses that ladder to list price only.</p>
  <p><code>stage4_causal.py</code> scores each surviving arm; the lab uses an S-learner that predicts expected margin. <code>stage5_bandit.py</code> is contextual Thompson sampling with an epsilon floor and a propensity floor so later OPE never divides by zero. <code>stage6_postprocess.py</code> charm-prices, binds a coupon, and applies stickiness so the same shopper and SKU can see the same offer again. <code>stage7_logging.py</code> writes the experience tuple, including propensity, without putting that tuple on the client response. <code>stage8_response.py</code> is the safe JSON the channel actually receives. <code>stage9_fallback.py</code> is the ladder used when a dependency is sick: you still return a price. <code>stage10_cache.py</code> holds the version pins (policy, causal model, guardrails) and supports hot reload.</p>
</section>

<section class="card" id="services">
  <p class="phase">Adapters</p>
  <h2>Services</h2>
  <p><code>src/pricing_decision/services/</code> is the seam you change when this lab becomes Azure. The orchestrator talks to these classes; the stages do not open files or sockets themselves.</p>
  <p><code>catalog.py</code> reads SKUs from <code>configs/catalog.yaml</code> today and will read Cosmos later. <code>identity.py</code> resolves a customer, guest, or anonymous id and the consent flag. <code>feature_store.py</code> is the in-memory map of feature vectors; Redis replaces it. <code>coupon.py</code> issues, looks up, and redeems offer codes; Cosmos becomes the ledger so a code still works after a policy change. <code>control_plane.py</code> holds the kill switch, merchandiser freeze, daily discount budget, and the sticky-price store; App Configuration and Redis take those jobs in production. <code>logger.py</code> appends JSONL under <code>data/log_buffer/</code> and already knows how to speak Kafka when <code>PDS_KAFKA_ENABLED</code> is true. <code>outcomes.py</code> records purchase, refund, and return against a <code>decision_id</code>. <code>gateway.py</code> is the in-process stand-in for the product split that Front Door and API Management will own: what is public versus what is explain and admin.</p>
</section>

<section class="card" id="core">
  <p class="phase">Shared types</p>
  <h2>Core</h2>
  <p><code>src/pricing_decision/core/</code> is the vocabulary the rest of the package shares. <code>models.py</code> is pydantic: the inbound <code>DecisionRequest</code>, arms, scores, the client <code>Offer</code>, the full <code>PricingDecision</code>, and the <code>DecisionContext</code> that travels down the pipeline. <code>exceptions.py</code> is how an unknown SKU becomes HTTP 404 and a validation failure becomes 400. <code>ids.py</code> mints <code>decision_id</code> values. <code>metrics.py</code> is the in-process counter snapshot behind <code>GET /metrics</code>. <code>tracing.py</code> is the hook for request timing. None of this knows about Azure.</p>
</section>

<section class="card" id="offline">
  <p class="phase">Night shift</p>
  <h2>Offline learning</h2>
  <p><code>src/pricing_decision/offline/</code> is the same product after checkout, when you are allowed to be slow. <code>pipeline.py</code> is the conductor: ingest, join, backfill, causal, bandit, OPE, registry, gate. <code>lake.py</code> reads and writes JSONL under <code>data/lake/</code>; that path becomes ADLS Delta later. <code>ingest.py</code> copies the live log buffer into the lake. <code>seed.py</code> can invent history so the lab has something to train on. <code>join.py</code> matches decisions to outcomes on <code>decision_id</code> with a reward window. <code>backfill.py</code> reconstructs features as of the decision timestamp, not “whatever is current.” <code>reward.py</code> turns a joined row into the scalar the models optimize.</p>
  <p><code>causal.py</code> trains the S-learner used online. <code>bandit.py</code> updates the policy. <code>ope.py</code> estimates IPS, SNIPS, and DR so you can score a new policy on old logs. <code>fairness.py</code> and <code>drift.py</code> are the gates that sit beside that estimate. <code>registry.py</code> writes <code>data/registry/models.json</code>; Azure ML replaces that file. <code>gate.py</code> decides whether a candidate is allowed to go near traffic. <code>rollout.py</code> is the shadow-then-canary story that Container Apps revisions will execute with traffic weights.</p>
</section>

<section class="card" id="glue">
  <p class="phase">How it is wired</p>
  <h2>Glue code</h2>
  <p><code>orchestrator.py</code> constructs every service and every stage, then <code>decide()</code> walks ingestion through response, catching failures into the fallback handler. <code>decide_batch()</code> is the campaign path. If you want to see the whole online story in one file, this is it.</p>
  <p><code>playground.py</code> powers the Online PDS tab: it can stop after a named stage so the lab can show arms or scores without finishing the request. <code>platform.py</code> powers Architecture: use cases from YAML, the monitor snapshot, CS lookup, the control-plane view. <code>architecture.py</code> loads the YAML that fills the Architecture, Azure, and Project left-navs.</p>
  <p><code>cli.py</code> is the command line. <code>pds serve</code> starts uvicorn. <code>pds decide -f examples/request.json --explain</code> runs one decision without a browser. That is the fastest way to prove the brain still works after you touch a stage.</p>
</section>

<section class="card" id="configs">
  <p class="phase">Knobs</p>
  <h2>configs</h2>
  <p>YAML in <code>configs/</code> is what the running process reads. Change a file and, for many of them, reload; you should not need a new function to add a SKU or flip a kill switch in the lab.</p>
  <p><code>catalog.yaml</code> is the demo merchandising world: Maya, James, Priya, Alex, Noah, and the SKUs including SKU-1234 at list 50. <code>segments.yaml</code> names those shopper types. <code>features.yaml</code> is the feature contract and TTLs. <code>guardrails.yaml</code> is MAP, floors, frequency, and budget. <code>ladders.yaml</code> is the discount arms. <code>control_plane.yaml</code> is kill switch, freeze, sticky TTL, and the daily cap. <code>versions.yaml</code> pins policy, causal model, and guardrail version. <code>stages.yaml</code> and <code>offline_stages.yaml</code> are the left-nav copy for the lab. <code>use_cases.yaml</code> is PDP, kill switch, sticky, budget, holdout, and the rest of the Architecture demos. <code>architecture.yaml</code> is layers, loops, and gaps. <code>azure_architecture.yaml</code>, <code>azure_components.yaml</code>, and <code>azure_stages.yaml</code> feed the Azure tab. <code>project_map.yaml</code> is the left-nav for this page.</p>
</section>

<section class="card" id="data">
  <p class="phase">What the lab writes</p>
  <h2>data</h2>
  <p>Nothing under <code>data/</code> is the source of truth for how the product should behave; it is what a run produced. You can delete the JSONL files and the lab will recreate them the next time you score or train. Do not hand-edit them and expect the models to stay coherent.</p>
  <p><code>data/log_buffer/decisions.jsonl</code> is the live experience log, one JSON object per <code>decide()</code>, including propensity. That file is what Event Hubs replaces. <code>data/lake/</code> is the local lakehouse: <code>decisions.jsonl</code> after ingest, <code>outcomes.jsonl</code> from checkout events, <code>training.jsonl</code> after join, <code>backfill.jsonl</code> after point-in-time features, plus <code>causal_model.jsonl</code>, <code>bandit_model.jsonl</code>, <code>ope_report.jsonl</code>, <code>fairness_report.jsonl</code>, and <code>drift_report.jsonl</code>. <code>data/registry/models.json</code> is the tiny model registry the gate reads. On Azure those paths become Event Hubs, ADLS, and Azure ML.</p>
</section>

<section class="card" id="tests">
  <p class="phase">Proof</p>
  <h2>tests</h2>
  <p><code>tests/conftest.py</code> builds a shared orchestrator fixture so each test does not re-parse every YAML file. The <code>test_stage*.py</code> files walk the online contract: ingestion, preprocess, guardrails and candidates, causal and bandit, response and logging. <code>test_stage_playground.py</code> hits the lab run API. <code>test_offline_pipeline.py</code> seeds, joins, and checks OPE. <code>test_architecture.py</code> is the net under the Architecture, Azure, and Project tabs — it asserts the HTML maps and the JSON catalogs still exist. From the Pricing folder, <code>pytest</code> should stay green after you change a stage. Azure integration tests, when you add them, belong here marked so they skip unless <code>PDS_ENV</code> starts with <code>azure</code>.</p>
</section>

<section class="card" id="infra">
  <p class="phase">Around the package</p>
  <h2>infra, docs, scripts, examples</h2>
  <p><code>infra/azure-up.ps1</code> is the one-pass deploy: resource group, ACR, Container Apps, a printed HTTPS URL. <code>infra/cli-kids.ps1</code> is the same first deploy with more prompting. Neither script rewrites Python. They host the Docker image of this package in Canada Central.</p>
  <p><code>docs/azure-implementation.html</code> is the Azure tab: components, architecture, CLI, phases. <code>docs/project-map.html</code> is this file. FastAPI serves both; you can also open them as files in a browser.</p>
  <p><code>examples/request.json</code> is a legal <code>POST /v1/price</code> body for the CLI. <code>scripts/</code> holds one-off helpers that were used to generate pieces of the Azure HTML. They are not part of the runtime. You do not run them to price anything.</p>
</section>
